title: Computational entanglement distillation beyond pure states: efficient protocols and fundamental limitations

paper.title: Computational entanglement distillation beyond pure states: efficient protocols and fundamental limitations
paper.abstract: Abstract The information-theoretic approach to entanglement typically relies on arbitrarily many input copies and unboundedly complex operations; however, the available resources are constrained in reality. This motivates the study of entanglement theory with limited resources. One of its central questions is which quantities characterize entanglement manipulations, and so far, only the idealized case of pure states has been well explored. In this work, we address entanglement distillation from mixed states and identify the Rényi coherent information as the quantity determining the optimal rate in the worst case under two distinct resource constraints. We first characterize the sample-efficient regime, in which unbounded computational power is allowed. Our universal protocol achieves this rate without knowledge of the input state under certain polynomial rank constraints. This rate is optimal among universal protocols: we construct states whose distillable entanglement is nearly extensive, yet from which no universal sample-efficient protocol attains a rate above their Rényi coherent information. We then push this characterization to the computationally efficient frontier: the same bound holds for any efficient protocol even when the input state is known, and another universal protocol achieves this rate efficiently under additional polynomial constraints on the marginal ranks. Overall, our results give the Rényi coherent information a novel operational meaning in two computational settings: universal distillation with limited copies and efficient distillation even with knowledge of the input state.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Quantum information theory characterizes the ultimate limits of information processing. Entanglement theory is a prime example: it studies how entanglement, a central resource of quantum information processing, can be quantified and manipulated under local operations and classical communication (LOCC) [ 1 ] . One of its most fundamental tasks is entanglement distillation, which converts multiple copies of a noisy entangled state into nearly perfect Bell pairs [ 2 , 3 ] . Distillation supplies resources for teleportation [ 4 ] , quantum repeaters [ 5 ] , and quantum cryptography [ 6 ] , and lies at the heart of quantum Shannon theory [ 7 ] , closely tied to quantum communication over noisy channels [ 3 ] . Which quantities characterize the optimal asymptotic distillation rate, known as the distillable entanglement, is a central question in entanglement theory. For pure states, this rate is given by the entanglement entropy [ 8 ] . Noisy states, however, are generally mixed, and their distillable entanglement is harder to characterize: a general closed-form expression is unknown, and some entangled states cannot be distilled at all [ 9 ] . The optimal distillation rate can nevertheless be characterized in terms of the coherent information [ 10 , 11 ] . These entropic characterizations, however, describe what is possible in principle rather than what is feasible in practice. Since physical resources are limited, accounting for the cost of manipulating entanglement is crucial. Specifically, what matters is how the number of copies and the complexity of operations scale with the number n n of qubits. Once efficiency is imposed by restricting both to grow polynomially with n n , the picture changes drastically [ 12 , 13 ] . This is illustrated by pseudoentanglement [ 14 ] , which extends quantum pseudorandomness [ 15 ] to entanglement and provides two ensembles with very different amounts of entanglement that no efficient observer can tell apart. Since efficient protocols cannot distinguish these ensembles, there exist states with large distillable entanglement from which they distill only a small amount. Such observations, together with the advance of quantum technologies toward practical use, have motivated computational entanglement theory, which seeks to characterize the limits attainable by efficient protocols and identifies computational counterparts of entanglement measures and entropic quantities [ 16 , 12 , 17 , 13 , 18 ] . For pure states, Leone et al. [ 12 ] recently showed that, with resources polynomial in n n , the optimal distillation rate is characterized in the worst case by the min-entropy of the reduced state rather than its von Neumann entropy. Yet pure states are highly idealized—the natural setting for distillation involves mixed states produced by noise. In the distillation protocol for pure states [ 19 ] on which Ref. [ 12 ] relies, simply measuring the Schur labels of the copies already leaves a maximally entangled state. In contrast, for mixed states we must deal with correlations with the environment, and an additional decoding step is needed to recover Bell pairs. The standard decoupling approach [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] to mixed-state distillation uses Uhlmann’s theorem [ 23 ] to guarantee the existence of a suitable decoder, known as the Uhlmann transformation, but this does not by itself yield an efficient implementation [ 24 ] . From the perspective of fundamental limitations, existing converse bounds indicate large gaps between information-theoretic and efficient distillation, but do not identify the quantity governing the efficient rate [ 25 , 26 ] . These facts leave open questions: how much entanglement can be distilled from mixed states under resource constraints, and which quantity characterizes the optimal rate? We answer these questions by showing that the sandwiched Rényi coherent information [ 27 , 28 ] of an intermediate order β ∈ ( 1 / 2 , 1 ) \beta\in(1/2,1) determines, in the worst case, the optimal distillation rate in two distinct settings with resource constraints. In the first setting, the number of copies is polynomial in the number n n of qubits, while the circuit size is unrestricted. Here we consider universal one-way LOCC distillation, which uses no description of the input state. The universal entanglement distillation was initially considered for pure-state inputs [ 19 ] and has recently been extended to general mixed states [ 29 , 30 , 31 ] . In particular, Rizzo et al. [ 29 ] generalized the protocol for pure states [ 19 ] to universal Schur coding for mixed states. For polynomial-rank states, their protocol achieves rates given by the Rényi coherent information capped at C ​ log ⁡ n C\log{n} for any constant C > 0 C>0 . We further extend this guarantee to any state close to a polynomial-rank state, including a low-rank state subject to weak noise, by making the decoder robust to deviations in a small fraction of the copies. The rate is then determined by the Rényi coherent information of this nearby state. While this protocol is sample-efficient, its efficient implementation remains open. We next turn to the second setting, in which the circuit size is also polynomial in n n . 1 1 1 Computationally efficient protocols are automatically sample-efficient, since a circuit of polynomial size can act on only polynomially many copies. Under the additional condition that the nearby state has polynomial marginal ranks, we obtain another universal one-way LOCC protocol based on decoupling that achieves the Rényi coherent information. Since known implementations of the Uhlmann transformation [ 32 , 33 ] become costly in high dimensions, our key idea is universal collective compression, which reduces the local dimension per copy to a polynomial. Under the marginal-rank condition, the compression loses almost no entanglement. The receiving party then learns the compressed state from some of the copies and efficiently implements the Uhlmann transformation on the others. To establish the optimality of these rates in the worst case, we construct a family of n n -qubit mixed states of polynomial rank whose information-theoretic distillable entanglement is as large as Ω ~ ​ ( n ) \widetilde{\Omega}(n) . For universal LOCC protocols using k = poly ⁡ ( n ) k=\mathrm{poly}(n) copies, the rate is capped by the smaller of the Rényi coherent information and log ⁡ k \log{k} , even when the circuit size is unrestricted. Its main ingredient is statistical indistinguishability: given polynomially many copies, ensembles constructed from Haar-random states cannot be distinguished from ensembles carrying little entanglement. The Schur-coding protocol nearly matches this bound, attaining the Rényi coherent information up to o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) when it is 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) {\mathcal{O}}(\log{n}) and otherwise a constant fraction of log ⁡ k \log{k} at the number k k of copies it uses. We next turn to the computationally efficient setting, now allowing the protocol to be tailored to the input state, and we show that the same bound holds even in this setting. The states in this construction, however, need not be efficiently preparable, so the bound may be attributed to the complexity of the states themselves [ 16 ] . Computational indistinguishability based on public-key pseudoentanglement [ 34 ] closes this loophole. Under a post-quantum hardness assumption for learning with errors (LWE) [ 35 ] , we construct efficiently preparable states for which a similar bound holds even against protocols efficiently compiled from a description of their preparation circuit, with log ⁡ k \log{k} replaced by a freely chosen function of order ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) \omega(\log{n}) . When the Rényi coherent information is 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) {\mathcal{O}}(\log{n}) , our efficient protocol attains the bound up to o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) without a description of the state. It is therefore optimal even against protocols tailored to the input state or efficiently compiled from a description of its preparation circuit. Our results reveal some features of efficient distillation that are specific to mixed states. First, intermediate Rényi orders are essential for characterizing the optimal rate of efficient distillation from mixed states. The Rényi coherent information at the endpoint β = 1 / 2 \beta=1/2 equals the min-entropy conditioned on the purifying system by the duality relation [ 27 ] . One might expect this endpoint to suffice for mixed states, as the min-entropy does for pure states [ 12 ] . For pure states, the trivial purifying system makes the values at all fixed orders β ∈ [ 1 / 2 , 1 ) \beta\in[1/2,1) agree up to a constant factor, whereas for mixed states these values can separate by an amount growing with the rank. Indeed, we construct polynomial-rank states whose conditional min-entropy is − Θ ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) -\Theta(\log{n}) , yet whose optimal rate of efficient distillation is Θ ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) \Theta(\log{n}) and attained by our efficient protocol up to o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) . More strongly, we find that every order in ( 1 / 2 , 1 ) (1/2,1) captures the optimal rate for some family of our states but misses it for another; hence, no single fixed order characterizes efficient distillation from mixed states. Second, the optimal rate of efficient distillation undergoes a sharp transition as the rank grows from polynomial to superpolynomial. At superpolynomial rank, our construction yields states from which no efficient protocol distills entanglement at all, even though their information-theoretic distillable entanglement remains Ω ~ ​ ( n ) \widetilde{\Omega}(n) . Such a transition was indicated for special classes of states in earlier work [ 25 , 26 ] ; our results establish it for general mixed states in the worst case. Finally, we mention that our results have implications across a broad range of areas in quantum information science. In quantum networks, decoding complexity is a practical bottleneck for distillation [ 36 ] , and noise on shared states is often not fully characterized. Our efficient protocol, which requires no description of the state, is a step toward addressing these problems. Beyond distillation, implementing the Uhlmann transformation in a compressed space may also facilitate decoding in quantum communication, state merging, and quantum information recovery [ 24 , 26 ] . Pseudoentanglement, in turn, connects our mixed-state constructions to quantum cryptography [ 37 ] and to questions of computational complexity in quantum gravity [ 14 , 38 ] , where mixed states play a central role [ 16 , 39 ] . Together, our protocols and constructions provide tools for investigating how resource constraints shape entanglement manipulation and its applications.

sections.heading: II.1 Achievability: Sample-efficient and computationally efficient protocols
sections.text: Our two distillation protocols apply to states ρ 𝖠𝖡 \rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} that are close to a state ρ ^ 𝖠𝖡 \hat{\rho}^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} of polynomial rank, in the sense that the trace distance 1 2 ​ ‖ ρ 𝖠𝖡 − ρ ^ 𝖠𝖡 ‖ 1 \frac{1}{2}\|\rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}}-\hat{\rho}^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}}\|_{1} is small. Their rates are determined by the Rényi coherent information I ~ β ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ρ ^ \widetilde{I}_{\beta}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\hat{\rho}} of the nearby state. The first protocol requires only a global-rank condition and is sample-efficient. The second is computationally efficient under an additional condition on the rank of Alice’s marginal. Both are universal: they use the promised rank bounds, a target rate, and the target error, but no description of either the input state ρ 𝖠𝖡 \rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} or the nearby state ρ ^ 𝖠𝖡 \hat{\rho}^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} . Theorem 1 (Achievability for mixed-state distillation; formal versions in Theorems 24 and 34 ) . (II) If rank ⁡ ( ρ ^ 𝖠𝖡 ) , rank ⁡ ( ρ ^ 𝖠 ) = poly ⁡ ( n ) \mathrm{rank}(\hat{\rho}^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}}),\,\mathrm{rank}(\hat{\rho}^{{\mathsf{A}}})=\mathrm{poly}(n) , then R ≥ I ~ β ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ρ ^ − o ( 1 ) R\geq\widetilde{I}_{\beta}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\hat{\rho}}-o(1) , and the protocol is efficiently implemented by a circuit of size poly ⁡ ( n ) \mathrm{poly}(n) . Since the rank conditions concern ρ ^ 𝖠𝖡 \hat{\rho}^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} alone, the input ρ 𝖠𝖡 \rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} itself may have large rank, as long as its weight is concentrated near a state of polynomial rank; a typical example is a low-rank state subject to weak noise. Such an input is distilled at the rate determined by the nearby state. Moreover, the protocols do not need to know which input they receive. A single protocol is determined by the rank bounds, a target rate, and the target error, and it serves every input close to a state that meets these bounds and has Rényi coherent information at least the target rate. This universality makes the protocols applicable even when the noise affecting a shared state is not fully characterized. The two cases differ in their rank requirements and computational guarantees. In (II), the protocol is computationally efficient, but the marginal-rank condition it requires bounds the Rényi coherent information by the logarithm of Alice’s marginal rank, I ~ β ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ρ ^ ≤ log rank ( ρ ^ 𝖠 ) = 𝒪 ( log n ) \widetilde{I}_{\beta}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\hat{\rho}}\leq\log{\mathrm{rank}(\hat{\rho}^{{\mathsf{A}}})}={\mathcal{O}}(\log{n}) . 3 3 3 Both marginal ranks are in fact polynomially bounded: the bound on Bob’s marginal follows from the global-rank bound and the bound on Alice’s marginal, since rank ⁡ ( ρ ^ 𝖡 ) ≤ rank ⁡ ( ρ ^ 𝖠𝖡 ) ​ rank ​ ( ρ ^ 𝖠 ) \mathrm{rank}(\hat{\rho}^{{\mathsf{B}}})\leq\mathrm{rank}(\hat{\rho}^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}})\mathrm{rank}(\hat{\rho}^{{\mathsf{A}}}) . Nearby states with Rényi coherent information of order ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) \omega(\log{n}) thus have superpolynomial marginal rank and are left to (I). Dropping the marginal-rank condition, (I) reaches the rate C ​ log ⁡ n C\log{n} for any constant C > 0 C>0 even in this regime, at the cost of an unrestricted circuit size. Below, we outline how the two protocols are constructed: (I) extends universal Schur coding to perturbed inputs, while (II) makes the decoupling approach efficient by first compressing the local systems of the copies. For details, see Appendix C for (I) and Appendix D for (II). For (I), we start from the universal Schur coding of Ref. [ 29 ] . Alice and Bob apply the Schur transform to their copies and measure the local Schur labels. Alice then measures her symmetric-group register, keeping a register of smaller dimension, and sends her label and the outcome to Bob, who applies a decoder determined by the two labels and this outcome, independent of the input state. The labels select subspaces, the Schur supports, whose permutation symmetry makes the local marginals flat, allowing one decoder to work uniformly on each support; the Rényi coherent information controls the weight outside them. From polynomially many copies of polynomial-rank states, this protocol distills at the Rényi coherent information, capped at order log ⁡ n \log{n} [ 29 ] . Our contribution to (I) is to extend this guarantee to inputs that are only close to a polynomial-rank state and may themselves have large rank. The guarantee for the nearby state does not transfer directly: a small deviation in each copy accumulates, and the tensor powers ρ ⊗ k \rho^{\otimes k} and ρ ^ ⊗ k \hat{\rho}^{\otimes k} can be far apart for polynomially many copies. We instead enlarge the Schur supports to include deviations on a small fraction of the copies, and bound both the size of the enlargement and the weight remaining outside the enlarged supports ( Lemma 23 ). A single decoder then distills from every such input at the rate of the nearby state, still from polynomially many copies ( Lemma 22 ). Finally, a concatenated stabilizer code suppresses the remaining error ( Lemma 18 ). The decoder, however, is specified through Kronecker coefficients on spaces whose dimension grows with the number of copies, and an efficient implementation remains open. For (II), we start from a different approach based on decoupling [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . In this approach, Alice applies a random measurement, retains a register 𝖲 {\mathsf{S}} , and sends the outcome to Bob. The decoupling theorem [ 22 ] guarantees that 𝖲 {\mathsf{S}} is approximately completely mixed and decoupled from the purifying system when its size is chosen according to the Rényi coherent information. Uhlmann’s theorem [ 23 ] then guarantees a decoder on Bob’s systems, the Uhlmann transformation, that recovers Bell pairs shared with 𝖲 {\mathsf{S}} . Known algorithms for this transformation [ 32 , 33 ] , however, become exponentially costly when applied directly to the original high-dimensional systems. To resolve this problem, our first step is universal collective compression ( Lemma 25 ). Alice and Bob reduce the local dimension per copy to a polynomial without learning the original eigenbases. The marginal-rank condition ensures that this compression preserves the nearby state, up to local isometries and a small error. The parties perform local tomography on some of these compressed copies, and Alice sends her outcomes to Bob so that he can estimate the joint compressed state. However, compression alone does not yet make the decoding efficient: decoupling many compressed copies jointly would produce exponentially many outcomes, and the cost of Bob’s decoder grows with their number. Alice thus measures in two stages ( Lemmas 28 and 29 ): she first shrinks each compressed copy separately, retaining its conditional entropy, and then decouples a block of the shrunken copies with only polynomially many outcomes. For the reported outcome, Bob computes the Uhlmann transformation from his estimate as the unitary factor of a polar decomposition. The tensor-product structure of the estimate allows this transformation to be implemented at a cost polynomial in the dimension of one compressed copy and the block length, without constructing a matrix on the full block explicitly ( Lemma 30 ). Finally, a concatenated stabilizer code again suppresses the remaining error. Together, these steps incur only o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) rate loss, and the protocol thus attains the rate in (II) with polynomially many copies and a polynomial-size circuit. All communication goes from Alice to Bob, and the circuit is computed from the promised rank bounds, the target rate, and the target error.

sections.heading: II.2 Converse: No-go results and optimality
sections.text: We now ask whether a different protocol can substantially improve these rates. Our converse results construct a family of states with large information-theoretic distillable entanglement but much lower rates under the resource constraints. To state what these bounds rule out, we also need to specify how a protocol may depend on the input state. We distinguish the following three models; see Definition 10 for the formal definition. • State-agnostic. A single protocol is required to succeed on every state in a prescribed set, without information about which member it receives. Its circuit size is unrestricted. • State-dependent. The protocol has polynomial circuit size and may depend on the state in any way; no account is taken of how the circuit is found. • Description-aware. An efficient compiler receives a classical description of a circuit C 𝖠𝖡𝖤 C^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}{\mathsf{E}}} preparing a purification of ρ 𝖠𝖡 \rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} , C 𝖠𝖡𝖤 ​ | 0 ⟩ 𝖠𝖡𝖤 = | ρ ⟩ 𝖠𝖡𝖤 C^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}{\mathsf{E}}}|0\rangle^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}{\mathsf{E}}}=|\rho\rangle^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}{\mathsf{E}}} , and outputs an efficient LOCC protocol. Here 𝖤 {\mathsf{E}} is the purifying system. A single compiler is required to succeed on all but a negligible fraction of preparation-circuit descriptions drawn from a given distribution. Thus, moving from state-agnostic to state-dependent models restricts computation while allowing arbitrary dependence on the state; the description-aware model further accounts for the cost of constructing the protocol. Our states consist of two components with separate roles: a tunable spike state ( Lemma 38 ) controls the Rényi coherent information, while a weakly weighted, highly entangled entanglement amplifier keeps E D ​ ( 𝖠 : 𝖡 ) ρ E_{\mathrm{D}}({\mathsf{A}}:{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho} nearly extensive. Following the pseudoentanglement-based approach of Refs. [ 14 , 16 , 34 , 40 , 12 ] , we make the amplifier indistinguishable from a weakly entangled counterpart. A resource-limited protocol cannot distill more entanglement from a hidden component than its counterpart holds, since its output would otherwise tell the two apart. The rate is thus capped by the Rényi coherent information set by the spike. The spike state provides Rényi coherent information only up to order 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) {\mathcal{O}}(\log{n}) ; for larger values, we replace the spike with a highly entangled state that is also indistinguishable from a counterpart with less entanglement. We choose these counterparts so that they remain indistinguishable from the high-entanglement states given any polynomial number k k of copies. How little entanglement such a counterpart may carry depends on the rank of our states, a free parameter that can be chosen without changing E D ​ ( 𝖠 : 𝖡 ) ρ E_{\mathrm{D}}({\mathsf{A}}:{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho} or the Rényi coherent information. At polynomial rank, the counterpart must still have entanglement of order ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) \omega(\log{n}) , which appears in the description-aware model as the second entry θ \theta of the cap in the following theorem. In the other two models, the second entry is instead θ = log ⁡ k \theta=\log{k} , obtained by a separate argument. At superpolynomial rank, the whole state can be hidden behind one with no distillable entanglement, and the rate drops to zero. 4 4 4 The converse bounds impose ε < 1 / 2 \varepsilon<1/2 and k = ω ⁡ ( 1 ) k=\omega(1) for the following reasons. Since a separable state can have fidelity 1 / 2 1/2 with a Bell pair, a protocol at ε ≥ 1 / 2 \varepsilon\geq 1/2 can declare 1 1 ebit without distilling any, and an upper bound of zero on the rate requires ε < 1 / 2 \varepsilon<1/2 . The number of ebits declared in this way is at most log ⁡ ( 1 / ( 1 − ε ) ) \log(1/(1-\varepsilon)) , and bounds of order o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) nevertheless hold for every constant ε < 1 \varepsilon<1 . More generally, m − t m-t Bell pairs together with a product state can have fidelity 2 − t 2^{-t} with m m Bell pairs; a fixed error thus allows a constant excess t t in the declared number of ebits, whose effect t / k t/k on the rate vanishes for k = ω ⁡ ( 1 ) k=\omega(1) . Theorem 2 (Converse for mixed-state distillation; formal versions in Theorems 49 , 50 and 59 ) . ( 245 ) and ( 297 )). By construction, E D ​ ( 𝖠 : 𝖡 ) ρ E_{\mathrm{D}}({\mathsf{A}}:{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho} and the Rényi coherent information equal those of ρ 0 𝖨 𝖠 ​ 𝖨 𝖡 \rho_{0}^{{\mathsf{I}}_{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{I}}_{\mathsf{B}}} , while rank ⁡ ( ρ 𝖠𝖡 ) \mathrm{rank}(\rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}}) is the number of labels times rank ⁡ ( ρ 0 𝖨 𝖠 ​ 𝖨 𝖡 ) \mathrm{rank}(\rho_{0}^{{\mathsf{I}}_{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{I}}_{\mathsf{B}}}) . The bounds in the three models rest on different types of indistinguishability: statistical in the first two, discussed in Appendix F , and computational in the third, discussed in Appendix G . In the first two models, the amplifier and its counterpart are drawn from Haar-random states and Haar-subsystem states, respectively, which cannot be distinguished from polynomially many copies, regardless of computational power [ 12 ] . Hence, the bounds in these models require no hardness assumption. In the state-agnostic model, where a single protocol must work throughout the state set, this indistinguishability alone gives the first entry of the cap, with no restriction on the circuit size. In the state-dependent model, the protocol may instead be tailored to a single state, and the bound then requires one state that defeats every such protocol. We select such a hard instance from the same set by concentration of measure and a union bound over polynomial-size circuits, which is where the circuit-size restriction enters. In the description-aware model, the compiler also receives a preparation-circuit description, so statistical indistinguishability of the copies alone does not suffice. Under the LWE hardness assumptions, public-key pseudoentanglement [ 34 , 40 ] instead supplies computational indistinguishability even given these descriptions. 5 5 5 The LWE assumptions are imposed at superpolynomial strength, and for binary secrets, to cover the widest parameter ranges. Under polynomial hardness, or with standard secrets, the smallest attainable θ \theta rises and the zero-rate case recedes to a larger rank, leaving the ranks in between uncovered. The bound E D ​ ( 𝖠 : 𝖡 ) ρ = Ω ~ ​ ( n ) E_{\mathrm{D}}({\mathsf{A}}:{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho}=\widetilde{\Omega}(n) would also weaken under polynomial hardness. The gap between E D ​ ( 𝖠 : 𝖡 ) ρ E_{\mathrm{D}}({\mathsf{A}}:{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho} and the rate of any efficient protocol remains in every case; we will discuss these points at the end of Sec. G.4 . The bound of Theorem 2 also reveals a phenomenon that has no counterpart for pure states: a sharp transition in the rank. As the second case in Eq. ( 2 ) shows, the rate of resource-limited protocols drops from the cap of the first case to zero once the rank becomes superpolynomial, while E D ​ ( 𝖠 : 𝖡 ) ρ E_{\mathrm{D}}({\mathsf{A}}:{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho} and I ~ β ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ρ \widetilde{I}_{\beta}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho} remain unchanged. Since ρ 0 𝖨 𝖠 ​ 𝖨 𝖡 \rho_{0}^{{\mathsf{I}}_{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{I}}_{\mathsf{B}}} has polynomial rank, superpolynomial rank means superpolynomially many labels in Eq. ( 4 ). Polynomially many copies then almost never share a label, and each copy is scrambled by its own local unitary. In the statistical construction, these unitaries are independent and Haar random, and the mixture becomes statistically indistinguishable from a separable state that is completely mixed on 𝖨 𝖠 ​ 𝖨 𝖡 {\mathsf{I}}_{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{I}}_{\mathsf{B}} ( Lemma 44 ). In the computational construction, they are Heisenberg–Weyl displacements that look independent and uniformly random to efficient observers, and the same indistinguishability holds computationally ( Lemma 57 ). No entanglement can be distilled from this separable state. This indistinguishability requires superpolynomial rank: at polynomial rank, the purity of the state is at least 1 / poly ⁡ ( n ) 1/\mathrm{poly}(n) , and a SWAP test efficiently distinguishes it from this separable state of purity 2 − Θ ⁡ ( n ) 2^{-\Theta(n)} . In fact, the bound of Theorem 2 holds in every model even if each party is additionally given l = poly ⁡ ( n ) l=\mathrm{poly}(n) copies of a purification | ρ ⟩ 𝖠𝖡𝖤 |\rho\rangle^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}{\mathsf{E}}} of ρ 𝖠𝖡 \rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} in its own local laboratory, which carry no entanglement across the cut 𝖠 | 𝖡 {\mathsf{A}}|{\mathsf{B}} . In the state-agnostic and state-dependent models, Theorems 49 and 50 include these local copies, with the second entry θ = log ⁡ k \theta=\log{k} replaced by log ⁡ ( k + 2 ​ l ) \log{(k+2l)} , since our arguments extend to the purifications. In the description-aware model, such copies add nothing, as the compiler can prepare them efficiently from the given circuit description. We now show that our protocols are optimal on suitable families of Theorem 2 . When the Rényi coherent information of ρ 𝖠𝖡 \rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} is ω ⁡ ( 1 ) \omega(1) and 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) {\mathcal{O}}(\log{n}) , both protocols attain the first entry of the cap up to o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) . To see this, note that removing the amplifier branch from ρ 0 𝖨 𝖠 ​ 𝖨 𝖡 \rho_{0}^{{\mathsf{I}}_{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{I}}_{\mathsf{B}}} in every term of Eq. ( 4 ) leaves a state ρ ^ 𝖠𝖡 \hat{\rho}^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} within trace distance η \eta of ρ 𝖠𝖡 \rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} . If ρ 𝖠𝖡 \rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} has polynomial rank, Eq. ( 4 ) has polynomially many labels. As only the spike state remains in each term, the global and marginal ranks of ρ ^ 𝖠𝖡 \hat{\rho}^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} are at most the number of labels times those of the spike state, and are hence polynomial, whereas the amplifier makes the marginal ranks of ρ 𝖠𝖡 \rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} exponential. The Rényi coherent information of ρ ^ 𝖠𝖡 \hat{\rho}^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} equals that of ρ 𝖠𝖡 \rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} up to o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) . With η ≤ 1 / log 1 + c ⁡ n \eta\leq 1/\log^{1+c}{n} for a constant c > 0 c>0 , ρ ^ 𝖠𝖡 \hat{\rho}^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} serves as the nearby state in both cases of Theorem 1 . In (I), we take C C large enough that C ​ log ⁡ n C\log{n} exceeds the Rényi coherent information of ρ ^ 𝖠𝖡 \hat{\rho}^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} . For larger Rényi coherent information, only (I) applies, and an estimate of its number of copies shows that its rate reaches any fixed fraction B < 1 / 2 B<1/2 of the second entry log ⁡ k \log{k} of the cap. We thus obtain the following corollary (see Appendix H for a detailed discussion). Corollary 3 (Worst-case optimality) . There exist polynomial-rank families { ρ 𝖠𝖡 } n \{\rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}}\}_{n} of Theorem 2 , with E D ​ ( 𝖠 : 𝖡 ) ρ = Ω ~ ​ ( n ) E_{\mathrm{D}}({\mathsf{A}}:{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho}=\widetilde{\Omega}(n) , for which the following statements on the universal protocols (I) and (II) of Theorem 1 hold at every fixed order β ∈ ( β c , 1 ) \beta\in(\beta_{\mathrm{c}},1) and every constant error ε ∈ ( 0 , 1 / 2 ) \varepsilon\in(0,1/2) , where optimality is taken among LOCC protocols acting on k k copies with ω ⁡ ( 1 ) ≤ k ≤ poly ⁡ ( n ) \omega(1)\leq k\leq\mathrm{poly}(n) . (i) If I ~ β ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ρ \widetilde{I}_{\beta}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho} is ω ⁡ ( 1 ) \omega(1) and 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) {\mathcal{O}}(\log{n}) , the rate of (I) is optimal up to o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) in the state-agnostic model, and that of (II) in all three models. In the description-aware model, the optimality of (II) holds for efficiently preparable families under the LWE assumptions of Theorem 2 . (ii) If I ~ β ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ρ \widetilde{I}_{\beta}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho} is ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) \omega(\log{n}) , then, for every constant B ∈ ( 0 , 1 / 2 ) B\in(0,1/2) , protocol (I) attains R ≥ B ​ log ⁡ k R\geq B\log{k} at the number of copies k = poly ⁡ ( n ) k=\mathrm{poly}(n) it uses, while the optimal rate in the state-agnostic model at this k k is at most log ⁡ k + o ⁡ ( 1 ) \log{k}+o(1) . As the spike state is tunable, the Rényi coherent information of the families in Corollary 3 can be set to any value between ω ⁡ ( 1 ) \omega(1) and 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) {\mathcal{O}}(\log{n}) up to o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) , and the guarantee R ≥ I ~ β ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ρ ^ − o ( 1 ) R\geq\widetilde{I}_{\beta}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\hat{\rho}}-o(1) of Theorem 1 cannot be improved at any value in this range. The protocols of Theorem 1 use only the rank bounds, the target rate, and the target error, which are common to all states of the prescribed set from which these families are selected. Hence both (I) and (II) work throughout the set, as the state-agnostic model requires. Protocol (II) has a polynomial-size circuit and thus also qualifies in the state-dependent model; as it uses no description of the state, it also qualifies in the description-aware model, where a compiler simply outputs our protocol regardless of the given description. The second entry θ \theta in the polynomial-rank case of Eq. ( 2 ) matters when the Rényi coherent information exceeds it. In the state-agnostic and state-dependent models, θ = log ⁡ k \theta=\log{k} comes from the local unitaries in Eq. ( 4 ), which are Haar random in the statistical construction. Averaging over them upper bounds the rate by log ⁡ k + o ⁡ ( 1 ) \log{k}+o(1) at every k k , for a family fixed independently of k k ( Lemma 44 ). By (ii) of Corollary 3 , the optimal rate in the state-agnostic model is Θ ⁡ ( log ⁡ k ) \Theta(\log{k}) at the number k k of copies used by (I), as for pure states [ 12 ] . In the description-aware model, θ \theta is instead the entanglement of the weakly entangled states behind which the highly entangled components are hidden. It can be any prescribed function of order ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) \omega(\log{n}) , and the families are chosen for this θ \theta . The order ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) \omega(\log{n}) cannot be reduced to 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) {\mathcal{O}}(\log{n}) by comparison with a computationally indistinguishable ensemble of polynomial rank whose distillation rate admits such an information-theoretic cap uniformly over polynomial numbers of copies: a polynomial-rank ensemble indistinguishable from states with Rényi coherent information ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) \omega(\log{n}) still allows (I) to distill at rate C ​ log ⁡ n C\log{n} for every constant C > 0 C>0 ( Proposition 61 ). Whether computationally efficient protocols match the cap in this regime remains open, as we obtain no efficient protocol without a nearby state of polynomial marginal rank. The other restriction in the converse concerns the Rényi order: the cap holds only above a threshold β c > 1 / 2 \beta_{\mathrm{c}}>1/2 , leaving a range of lower orders uncovered. Whether this exclusion is an artifact of our construction or is genuine for mixed states, and more broadly whether a single fixed order suffices to characterize efficient distillation from mixed states, are the questions of the next subsection.

sections.text: Our rates are expressed by the Rényi coherent information I ~ β ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ρ \widetilde{I}_{\beta}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho} at a fixed order β < 1 \beta<1 . The guarantee of Theorem 1 holds at every order β ∈ [ 1 / 2 , 1 ) \beta\in[1/2,1) , while the cap of Theorem 2 holds only above the threshold β c \beta_{\mathrm{c}} . We now ask which Rényi orders β \beta are singled out by efficient distillation from mixed states. The two end points of the range have clear meanings: as β → 1 \beta\to 1 , the Rényi coherent information tends to the coherent information, which is achievable without any resource constraint [ 11 ] ; at β = 1 / 2 \beta=1/2 , it becomes the conditional min-entropy given the purifying system 𝖤 {\mathsf{E}} of ρ 𝖠𝖡 \rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} , i.e., I ~ 1 / 2 ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ρ = H min ( 𝖠 | 𝖤 ) ρ \widetilde{I}_{1/2}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho}=H_{\rm min}({\mathsf{A}}|{\mathsf{E}})_{\rho} [ 27 ] , which for pure states reduces to the min-entropy characterizing distillation with limited resources [ 12 ] . For pure states, this question does not arise, since the Rényi coherent information at every fixed order agrees with the min-entropy up to a constant factor. To see this, we provide the following relation that bounds how far the Rényi coherent information can lie above its value at β = 1 / 2 \beta=1/2 . While this relation follows from a direct calculation, for completeness we derive it in Appendix I . Proposition 4 (Rank bound on the separation of Rényi orders) . For any state ϱ 𝖠𝖡 \varrho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} and β ∈ ( 1 / 2 , 1 ) \beta\in(1/2,1) , I ~ 1 / 2 ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ϱ ≤ I ~ β ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ϱ ≤ β 1 − β ( I ~ 1 / 2 ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ϱ + 2 log rank ( ϱ 𝖠𝖡 ) ) . \displaystyle\widetilde{I}_{1/2}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\varrho}\leq\widetilde{I}_{\beta}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\varrho}\leq\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}\big(\widetilde{I}_{1/2}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\varrho}+2\log{\mathrm{rank}(\varrho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}})}\big). (5) From this proposition, we see that, for pure states, where rank ⁡ ( ρ 𝖠𝖡 ) = 1 \mathrm{rank}(\rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}})=1 , all fixed orders β ∈ [ 1 / 2 , 1 ) \beta\in[1/2,1) lie within a constant factor of the min-entropy H min ​ ( 𝖠 ) ρ H_{\rm min}({\mathsf{A}})_{\rho} . For mixed states, the extra term 2 ​ log ⁡ rank ​ ( ϱ 𝖠𝖡 ) 2\log{\mathrm{rank}(\varrho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}})} leaves room for different orders to separate. We next show that efficient distillation from mixed states reflects this separation. To this end, we again use the construction of the families of Theorem 2 , in which the Rényi coherent information of the spike state is tuned by two parameters β c , β s \beta_{\mathrm{c}},\beta_{\mathrm{s}} such that 1 / 2 < β s < β c < 1 1/2<\beta_{\mathrm{s}}<\beta_{\mathrm{c}}<1 ( Lemma 38 ). To leading order in the logarithm of the rank of the spike state, this quantity is constant for β c ≤ β < 1 \beta_{\mathrm{c}}\leq\beta<1 , decreases as β \beta decreases below β c \beta_{\mathrm{c}} , and changes sign at β = β s \beta=\beta_{\mathrm{s}} . We place a spike state of rank r − 1 r-1 in ρ 0 𝖨 𝖠 ​ 𝖨 𝖡 \rho_{0}^{{\mathsf{I}}_{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{I}}_{\mathsf{B}}} of Eq. ( 3 ) and take Eq. ( 4 ) with a single label; the resulting state ρ 𝖠𝖡 \rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} has rank r r . The following theorem shows that the efficient cap is then given by the Rényi coherent information at every order above β c \beta_{\mathrm{c}} . Below β c \beta_{\mathrm{c}} , the Rényi coherent information is smaller than the cap, and below β s \beta_{\mathrm{s}} it is even negative. Since β c \beta_{\mathrm{c}} and β s \beta_{\mathrm{s}} can be chosen freely, the orders at which these changes occur can be placed anywhere in ( 1 / 2 , 1 ) (1/2,1) . Theorem 5 (Separation) . For every pair of constants 1 / 2 < β s < β c < 1 1/2<\beta_{\mathrm{s}}<\beta_{\mathrm{c}}<1 and every r r satisfying ω ⁡ ( 1 ) ≤ r ≤ poly ⁡ ( n ) \omega(1)\leq r\leq\mathrm{poly}(n) , there is a family of mixed states { ρ 𝖠𝖡 } n \{\rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}}\}_{n} of Theorem 2 with rank ⁡ ( ρ 𝖠𝖡 ) = r \mathrm{rank}(\rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}})=r that exhibits the following two gaps: (1) the Rényi coherent information I ~ β ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ρ \widetilde{I}_{\beta}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho} changes sign at β = β s \beta=\beta_{\mathrm{s}} : it is + Θ ⁡ ( log ⁡ r ) +\Theta(\log{r}) for every fixed β ∈ ( β s , 1 ) \beta\in(\beta_{\mathrm{s}},1) and − Θ ⁡ ( log ⁡ r ) -\Theta(\log{r}) for every fixed β ∈ [ 1 / 2 , β s ) \beta\in[1/2,\beta_{\mathrm{s}}) ; (2) E D ​ ( 𝖠 : 𝖡 ) ρ = n Ω ⁡ ( 1 ) E_{\mathrm{D}}({\mathsf{A}}:{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho}=n^{\Omega(1)} , yet, for every constant ε < 1 / 2 \varepsilon<1/2 and ω ⁡ ( 1 ) ≤ k ≤ poly ⁡ ( n ) \omega(1)\leq k\leq\mathrm{poly}(n) , the rate R R of distillation from k k copies at error ε \varepsilon in the models specified below is at most I ~ β ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ρ + o ( 1 ) \widetilde{I}_{\beta}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho}+o(1) for any fixed β ∈ ( β c , 1 ) \beta\in(\beta_{\mathrm{c}},1) . Here, the rate bound holds in the state-agnostic and state-dependent models. Under the superpolynomial hardness of LWE with binary secrets ( Assumption 53 ), the family can be chosen to be efficiently preparable, and the rate bound then holds in the description-aware model. Each state of the family in Theorem 5 indeed admits a nearby state of polynomial global and marginal ranks whose Rényi coherent information agrees with the cap in (2) up to o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) . Protocol (II) of Theorem 1 then attains this cap at any fixed order β ∈ ( β c , 1 ) \beta\in(\beta_{\mathrm{c}},1) , and the optimal efficient rate is thus I ~ β ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ρ + o ( 1 ) = Θ ( log r ) \widetilde{I}_{\beta}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho}+o(1)=\Theta(\log{r}) at these orders. As the Rényi coherent information is smaller than this rate below β c \beta_{\mathrm{c}} , the exclusion of the orders below β c \beta_{\mathrm{c}} in Theorem 2 is genuine: for these states, a cap at any such order, including the endpoint β = 1 / 2 \beta=1/2 , would be violated. Since ρ 𝖠𝖡 \rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} has rank r r , the gap Θ ⁡ ( log ⁡ r ) \Theta(\log{r}) between the Rényi coherent information at orders above β c \beta_{\mathrm{c}} and the conditional min-entropy is the largest, up to constant factors, that Eq. ( 5 ) permits at that rank. In particular, at r = n Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) r=n^{\Theta(1)} , the optimal efficient rate and the conditional min-entropy are Θ ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) \Theta(\log{n}) and − Θ ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) -\Theta(\log{n}) , respectively. Since β c \beta_{\mathrm{c}} and β s \beta_{\mathrm{s}} can be chosen freely, any two fixed orders can be separated in this way. For any 1 / 2 ≤ β 2 < β 1 < 1 1/2\leq\beta_{2}<\beta_{1}<1 , choosing β 2 < β s < β c < β 1 \beta_{2}<\beta_{\mathrm{s}}<\beta_{\mathrm{c}}<\beta_{1} yields a family of states { ρ 𝖠𝖡 } n \{\rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}}\}_{n} with I ~ β 1 ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ρ = Θ ( log r ) , I ~ β 2 ( 𝖠 ⟩ 𝖡 ) ρ = − Θ ( log r ) , \displaystyle\widetilde{I}_{\beta_{1}}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho}=\Theta(\log{r}),\qquad\widetilde{I}_{\beta_{2}}({\mathsf{A}}\rangle{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho}=-\Theta(\log{r}), (6) where the former equals the optimal efficient rate up to o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) . Hence, every order β \beta in ( 1 / 2 , 1 ) (1/2,1) captures the optimal efficient rate for some family but misses it for another, even up to constant factors. We can conclude that no single fixed order characterizes efficient distillation from mixed states. This cannot occur for pure states, where all fixed orders agree up to constant factors by Proposition 4 , and is thus specific to mixed states. The negative conditional min-entropy above is the case β 2 = 1 / 2 \beta_{2}=1/2 . Finally, we focus on the gap between information-theoretic and efficient distillation. We can tune the spike state to make this gap nearly maximal: at β c − 1 / 2 = o ⁡ ( 1 / log ⁡ n ) \beta_{\mathrm{c}}-1/2=o(1/\log{n}) , the spike state becomes separable. Its Rényi coherent information tends to zero at every fixed order β ∈ [ 1 / 2 , 1 ) \beta\in[1/2,1) , closing the separation between different orders. The efficient rate then becomes o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) , while the entanglement amplifier keeps the information-theoretic distillable entanglement nearly extensive. The rank is again set by the number of labels in Eq. ( 4 ). It can be taken down to r = 1 r=1 , for which we omit the spike and obtain a pure state (see Appendix I for details). Proposition 6 (Nearly maximal separation; formal version in Proposition 62 ) . For every r r with 1 ≤ r ≤ poly ⁡ ( n ) 1\leq r\leq\mathrm{poly}(n) , there is a family of Θ ⁡ ( n ) \Theta(n) -qubit states { ρ 𝖠𝖡 } n \{\rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}}\}_{n} with rank ⁡ ( ρ 𝖠𝖡 ) = r \mathrm{rank}(\rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}})=r , such that E D ​ ( 𝖠 : 𝖡 ) ρ = Ω ~ ​ ( n ) E_{\mathrm{D}}({\mathsf{A}}:{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho}=\widetilde{\Omega}(n) , yet, for every constant ε < 1 \varepsilon<1 and ω ⁡ ( 1 ) ≤ k ≤ poly ⁡ ( n ) \omega(1)\leq k\leq\mathrm{poly}(n) , the rate R R of distillation from k k copies at error ε \varepsilon in the models specified below is o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) . Here, the bound holds in the state-agnostic and state-dependent models. Under the superpolynomial hardness of LWE with binary secrets ( Assumption 53 ), the family can be chosen to be efficiently preparable, and the bound then holds in the description-aware model. The same construction as in Theorem 5 thus also reproduces the nearly maximal separation known for pure states [ 12 ] , at every rank up to poly ⁡ ( n ) \mathrm{poly}(n) . At superpolynomial rank, Theorem 2 strengthens the worst-case conclusion to zero distilled ebits, while E D ​ ( 𝖠 : 𝖡 ) ρ E_{\mathrm{D}}({\mathsf{A}}:{\mathsf{B}})_{\rho} remains Ω ~ ​ ( n ) \widetilde{\Omega}(n) , in line with related separations shown for special classes of states in earlier work [ 25 , 26 ] . Hence, at every rank, efficiency can reduce a distillable entanglement of Ω ~ ​ ( n ) \widetilde{\Omega}(n) to a vanishing rate in the worst case. Note that these are limitations exhibited by the constructed families: rank alone does not preclude efficient distillation from an arbitrary mixed state.

sections.heading: III Discussion
sections.text: We have shown that, under rank conditions, entanglement can be distilled from mixed states at a rate determined by the Rényi coherent information, without using a description of the state. With polynomially many copies, the Schur-coding protocol [ 29 ] attains this rate for polynomial-rank states, capped at any rate that grows logarithmically with the number of qubits, and we have extended this guarantee to states close to a polynomial-rank state. When the nearby state also has polynomial marginal ranks, our decoupling-based protocol attains the rate by a polynomial-size circuit. Conversely, we have constructed states from which every protocol using polynomially many copies in the state-agnostic model distills essentially at most this rate, whatever its circuit size. The Schur-coding protocol is thus nearly optimal in this model. The same bound holds for efficient protocols tailored to the state and, under hardness assumptions on LWE, a similar one for those efficiently compiled from a description of the preparation circuit. When the Rényi coherent information is at most of order log ⁡ n \log{n} , our decoupling-based protocol attains this bound without any description of the state, and is therefore optimal even against such protocols. Once the rank of these states is superpolynomial, no efficient protocol distills any entanglement, although their information-theoretic distillable entanglement stays almost extensive at every rank. The rank thus marks a sharp transition in the computational distillable entanglement, one that is invisible from an information-theoretic perspective. Conceptually, our results show that efficient distillation still admits an entropic characterization, with the coherent information, which governs distillation without resource constraints, replaced by its Rényi generalization. Two further implications emerge from these results. First, in the worst case, knowledge of the state brings no advantage to efficient distillation: a protocol that uses no description of the state does as well as one tailored to the state or efficiently compiled from a description of its preparation circuit. The observation that protocols tailored to the state have no advantage over universal ones has been obtained in information-theoretic distillation [ 19 , 30 , 31 ] and in computational distillation from pure states [ 12 ] ; our results extend it to computational distillation from mixed states. Second, mixed states reveal a structure that pure states hide. For pure states, where the Rényi coherent information at all fixed orders β ∈ [ 1 / 2 , 1 ) \beta\in[1/2,1) agrees up to a constant factor, efficiency turns the min-entropy from a one-shot quantity into the rate of distillation from many copies [ 12 ] . For mixed states, this role passes to the Rényi coherent information of an intermediate order, which can be positive and attainable even when the conditional min-entropy is negative. Moreover, the relevant order depends on the state, and no single fixed order characterizes the rate for all mixed states. This change in the quantity characterizing the rate appears only beyond pure states. Our results point to several directions for future work. The most immediate question is whether efficient protocols can achieve a rate determined by the Rényi coherent information without the condition on the marginal ranks. This condition stems from compressing the local systems to polynomial dimension in our efficient protocol, whereas the Schur-coding protocol attains the rate without it from polynomially many copies. The remaining obstacle is thus purely computational, and it is unclear whether it reflects a genuine barrier or only a limitation of our approach. Removing the condition would extend our results to settings such as communication over quantum channels, where the sender’s marginal typically has high rank. Another question concerns the upper bounds for protocols efficiently compiled from a description of the preparation circuit, which rely on the hardness of LWE. Whether similar bounds and parameter ranges can be obtained under weaker assumptions, and which kind of computational hardness is necessary to keep entanglement inaccessible to such protocols, remain open. More broadly, one may ask which structures beyond rank make entanglement efficiently accessible: our converse is a worst-case statement, and a tensor product of many two-qubit Werner states, for instance, has exponentially large rank yet can be distilled efficiently at a constant rate per pair [ 36 ] . sections.heading: Appendix A Preliminaries
sections.text: We collect the notation used throughout this paper in Sec. A.1 . We define entanglement distillation protocols, the computational models, the corresponding distillable entanglements, and relate these measures in Sec. A.2 . In Sec. A.3 , we describe the conventions on precision for implementing operations with finite computational resources.

sections.heading: A.1 Notation
sections.text: In this work, we exclusively consider finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces ℋ {\mathcal{H}} , equipped with the standard inner product. We denote a physical system, also called a register, by a sans-serif letter such as 𝖠 {\mathsf{A}} , and its associated Hilbert space by ℋ 𝖠 {\mathcal{H}}^{\mathsf{A}} . We denote the dimension of a Hilbert space ℋ {\mathcal{H}} by dim ℋ \dim{\mathcal{H}} , abbreviated as d 𝖠 ≔ dim ℋ 𝖠 d_{\mathsf{A}}\coloneqq\dim{\mathcal{H}}^{\mathsf{A}} for a system 𝖠 {\mathsf{A}} . We mostly consider bipartite systems consisting of subsystems 𝖠 {\mathsf{A}} and 𝖡 {\mathsf{B}} , with Hilbert space ℋ 𝖠𝖡 = ℋ 𝖠 ⊗ ℋ 𝖡 {\mathcal{H}}^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}}={\mathcal{H}}^{\mathsf{A}}\otimes{\mathcal{H}}^{\mathsf{B}} . In particular, we focus on extensive bipartitions, where the numbers of qubits in 𝖠 {\mathsf{A}} and 𝖡 {\mathsf{B}} are of the same order. For an integer k ≥ 1 k\geq 1 , we write 𝖠 k {\mathsf{A}}^{k} for k k copies of 𝖠 {\mathsf{A}} , whose Hilbert space is ( ℋ 𝖠 ) ⊗ k ({\mathcal{H}}^{\mathsf{A}})^{\otimes k} . We write ℬ ⁡ ( ℋ ) {\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}) for the set of linear operators on ℋ {\mathcal{H}} . For any operator M M on ℋ {\mathcal{H}} , we denote the complex conjugate and the transpose in a given orthonormal basis by M ∗ M^{*} and M ⊤ M^{\top} , respectively, and denote the Hermitian conjugate by M † M^{\dagger} . A positive semidefinite operator ρ \rho with unit trace is called a quantum state. We say that a quantum state ψ \psi is pure if rank ⁡ ( ψ ) = 1 \mathrm{rank}(\psi)=1 . Pure states are also denoted by | ψ ⟩ ​ ⟨ ψ | |\psi\rangle\langle\psi| , or by the corresponding unit vector | ψ ⟩ |\psi\rangle . We denote a bipartite state of systems 𝖠𝖡 {\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}} by ρ 𝖠𝖡 \rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} and its reduced density matrices of systems 𝖠 {\mathsf{A}} and 𝖡 {\mathsf{B}} by ρ 𝖠 = Tr 𝖡 ⁡ [ ρ 𝖠𝖡 ] \rho^{\mathsf{A}}=\tr_{\mathsf{B}}[\rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}}] and ρ 𝖡 = Tr 𝖠 ⁡ [ ρ 𝖠𝖡 ] \rho^{\mathsf{B}}=\tr_{\mathsf{A}}[\rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}}] , respectively. A special class of bipartite states is given by maximally entangled states. We denote the maximally entangled state of Schmidt rank d d by | Φ d ⟩ 𝖠𝖡 ≔ 1 d ​ ∑ i = 1 d | i ⟩ 𝖠 ​ | i ⟩ 𝖡 , \displaystyle|\Phi_{d}\rangle^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}}\coloneqq\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}|i\rangle^{\mathsf{A}}|i\rangle^{\mathsf{B}}, (7) where { | i ⟩ } i \{|i\rangle\}_{i} is the computational basis. The state | Φ 2 ⟩ 𝖠𝖡 |\Phi_{2}\rangle^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} represents a Bell pair. We sometimes drop the subscript d d when it is clear from the context. Denoting the identity operator by 𝕀 {\mathbb{I}} , we write π 𝖠 ≔ 𝕀 𝖠 / d 𝖠 \pi^{\mathsf{A}}\coloneqq{\mathbb{I}}^{\mathsf{A}}/d_{\mathsf{A}} for the completely mixed state on system 𝖠 {\mathsf{A}} . A quantum channel from 𝖠 {\mathsf{A}} to 𝖠 ′ {\mathsf{A}}^{\prime} is denoted by 𝒯 𝖠 → 𝖠 ′ {\mathcal{T}}^{{\mathsf{A}}\to{\mathsf{A}}^{\prime}} , which is a completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) map acting on operators in the corresponding Hilbert spaces. We denote by id {\mathrm{id}} the identity channel. In this manuscript, we primarily focus on local operations and classical communication (LOCC) channels defined with respect to a fixed bipartition. These channels are composed of sequential applications of local quantum channels on subsystems, interleaved with rounds of classical communication. We omit the superscripts indicating systems or registers when they are clear from the context. Likewise, when no confusion arises, we omit the identity operator and the identity channel on the remaining systems, e.g., writing 𝒯 𝖡 → 𝖢 ​ ( σ 𝖡 ​ ρ 𝖠𝖡 ) {\mathcal{T}}^{{\mathsf{B}}\to{\mathsf{C}}}(\sigma^{\mathsf{B}}\rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}}) for ( id 𝖠 ⊗ 𝒯 𝖡 → 𝖢 ) ​ ( ( 𝕀 𝖠 ⊗ σ 𝖡 ) ​ ρ 𝖠𝖡 ) ({\mathrm{id}}^{\mathsf{A}}\otimes{\mathcal{T}}^{{\mathsf{B}}\to{\mathsf{C}}})\big(({\mathbb{I}}^{\mathsf{A}}\otimes\sigma^{\mathsf{B}})\rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}}\big) . Other fundamental quantities in quantum information are distance measures. For an operator M M , ‖ M ‖ p \|M\|_{p} with p ∈ ( 0 , ∞ ) p\in(0,\infty) denotes the Schatten p p -norm, defined as ‖ M ‖ p ≔ ( Tr ⁡ | M | p ) 1 / p \|M\|_{p}\coloneqq(\tr|M|^{p})^{1/p} . The Schatten p p -norm is nonincreasing in p p : ‖ M ‖ p ≤ ‖ M ‖ q \|M\|_{p}\leq\|M\|_{q} , for p ≥ q p\geq q . The distance admits the variational form 1 2 ​ ‖ ρ − σ ‖ 1 = max 0 ≤ Π ≤ 𝕀 ⁡ Tr ⁡ [ Π ⁡ ( ρ − σ ) ] \frac{1}{2}\|\rho-\sigma\|_{1}=\max_{0\leq\Pi\leq{\mathbb{I}}}\tr[\Pi(\rho-\sigma)] . To study distillation with limited resources, we need to specify both the resource constraints and how a protocol may depend on the input state. We first introduce the resource constraints. Efficiency is a property of a family indexed by n n , so Refs. [ 16 , 12 ] specify computational measures not by a value but by the function bounds that efficient families do and do not achieve. We instead carry the size bound s s as a parameter, as Ref. [ 17 ] does for the computational entropies: at a fixed s s , the class of protocols defined below is finite. Quantifying over s = poly ⁡ ( n ) s=\mathrm{poly}(n) outside the definition recovers the standard asymptotic notion of efficiency. Under resource constraints, additional local access to the state may help the parties, and our converse bounds hold even when they are given such access. We call a family of protocols indexed by n n sample-efficient if it acts on k = poly ⁡ ( n ) k=\mathrm{poly}(n) shared copies and l = poly ⁡ ( n ) l=\mathrm{poly}(n) additional local copies per party, with no restriction on its circuit size, and computationally efficient if, in addition, each member lies in 𝔏 ⁡ ( s , k , l ) \mathfrak{L}(s,k,l) with s = poly ⁡ ( n ) s=\mathrm{poly}(n) . We next introduce the computational models considered in this work. Definition 10 (Computational models) . A computational model specifies how a k k -shot distillation protocol may depend on the state it acts on. We consider the following three. (M1) State-agnostic : a single protocol, of unrestricted size, acts on every state of a prescribed set and receives no information about which one it is given. (M2) State-dependent : the protocol is implemented by an LOCC circuit of bounded size and may otherwise depend on the state in any way whatsoever, no account being taken of how it is found. (M3) Description-aware : the state carries a purification prepared by a known circuit, and the protocol is output by a single circuit of bounded size on input a classical description of that circuit. Model (M1) is the state-agnostic setting of Ref. [ 12 ] and formalizes universal distillation; its unrestricted size isolates the limitation due to the number of copies. Model (M2), defined for nonuniform circuit families, underlies the computational distillable entanglement of Refs. [ 16 , 12 ] , whose fixed-error regime is recovered here at a constant error. Model (M3) is adopted in the uniform computational measure of Ref. [ 16 ] , where the key indexing the family is passed as input to the protocol; in Ref. [ 34 ] the description is passed to the distinguisher instead. We first define the distillable entanglement in model (M1), where a single protocol must work for every state in a prescribed set, with no restriction on its circuit size. sections.heading: A.3 Finite precision and circuit compilation

The circuit size in Definition 9 counts gates from a finite set, while our constructions are described in ideal terms, such as an exact isometry, a unitary drawn from the Haar measure, or a tolerance given as a real number. None of these is realized by finitely many gates and bits as it stands. We hence provide in this subsection the prescriptions by which an ideal description is turned into a finite circuit, together with the accounting of the resulting errors. A reader interested only in the ideal protocol and familiar with this circuit compilation may proceed to Appendix B . Numerical data are represented by dyadic rationals, with positive tolerances rounded down to within a factor of two and loop bounds rounded up using certified bounds on logarithms and roots [ 50 ] . We call the errors of evaluating numerical quantities under these conventions arithmetic errors. For quantum operations, we take the finite gate set of Definition 9 to be inverse-closed and to contain the standard Clifford generators exactly, together with determinant-one one-qubit generators dense in SU ⁡ ( 2 ) \mathrm{SU}(2) . The constructive Solovay–Kitaev algorithm [ 51 ] synthesizes a circuit containing N 0 N_{0} gates outside this set to total operator error at most δ \delta using 𝒪 ⁡ ( N 0 ​ log 4 ⁡ ( N 0 / δ ) ) {\mathcal{O}}(N_{0}\log^{4}{(N_{0}/\delta)}) gates and polynomial classical overhead. Since a controlled call of a unitary turns its global phase into a relative one, we approximate it together with its phase. Before synthesis, we extend it to a determinant-one unitary on the original register and initialized work registers, which fixes the phase and is preserved by the gate set above. The ideal extension returns the work registers to zero. To bound the total approximation error, we mainly measure the error of each implementation by the diamond distance from the ideal operation. The distance is subadditive under composition [ 43 ] , so a circuit making at most G 0 G_{0} implementation calls stays within δ \delta of the ideal one if each call is accurate to δ / ( 1 + G 0 ) \delta/(1+G_{0}) . For adaptive circuits, the composition bound applies after the classical outcome registers are included in the channel description. Finite-gate and arithmetic errors are counted within the error budget of each construction, alongside its deliberate approximations. For uniform sampling, finitely many random bits produce an exact uniform distribution only when the size of the set is a power of two. We hence use rejection sampling with a fixed trial limit [ 52 , Sec. 9.2] . For a set of size m ≥ 2 m\geq 2 , we draw ⌈ log ⁡ m ⌉ \lceil\log{m}ceil random bits and reject values outside the set, so that each trial succeeds with probability at least 1 / 2 1/2 . For ζ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \zeta\in(0,1) , a limit of ⌈ log ⁡ ( 1 / ζ ) ⌉ \lceil\log{(1/\zeta)}ceil trials bounds the failure probability by ζ \zeta , and returning a fixed element on failure changes the output distribution by total variation at most ζ \zeta . For m = 1 m=1 , we return the sole element. Over at most R 0 R_{0} sampling calls, a failure probability of at most δ / ( 1 + R 0 ) \delta/(1+R_{0}) per call contributes at most δ \delta to the diamond distance, even when subsequent operations depend on the sampled labels. A finite-precision construction works with a matrix near the ideal one rather than the ideal matrix itself. The following lemma bounds the resulting displacement of the isometric factor of the thin QR factorization, with an amplification governed by the smallest singular value. This is used in the following two lemmas to implement a given isometry and a Haar unitary with finite precision. Lemma 15 (Perturbation of the isometric factor) . Let X X be a d × q d	imes q matrix with q ≤ d q\leq d , and suppose that its minimum singular value σ min ​ ( X ) \sigma_{\min}(X) satisfies σ min ​ ( X ) ≥ g > 0 \sigma_{\min}(X)\geq g>0 . Let Q ⁡ ( X ) Q(X) denote the isometric factor of its positive-diagonal thin QR factorization. Then, every matrix E E of the same size with ‖ E ‖ ∞ ≤ g / 2 \|E\|_{\infty}\leq g/2 satisfies ‖ Q ⁡ ( X + E ) − Q ⁡ ( X ) ‖ 2 ≤ 2 ​ 2 g ​ ‖ E ‖ 2 . \displaystyle\|Q(X+E)-Q(X)\|_{2}\leq rac{2\sqrt{2}}{g}\|E\|_{2}. (18) Proof of Lemma 15 . Since σ min ​ ( X + v ​ E ) ≥ g / 2 \sigma_{\min}(X+vE)\geq g/2 for 0 ≤ v ≤ 1 0\leq v\leq 1 , we may write X + v ​ E = Q v ​ R v X+vE=Q_{v}R_{v} with Q v Q_{v} and R v R_{v} differentiable in v v , and denote the derivatives by Q ˙ v \dot{Q}_{v} and R ˙ v \dot{R}_{v} . Since R v R_{v} has the same singular values as X + v ​ E X+vE , we have ‖ R v − 1 ‖ ∞ ≤ 2 / g \|R_{v}^{-1}\|_{\infty}\leq 2/g , and hence ‖ Q ⁡ ( X + E ) − Q ⁡ ( X ) ‖ 2 = ‖ ∫ 0 1 Q ˙ v ​ 𝑑 v ‖ 2 ≤ 2 ​ ∫ 0 1 ‖ E ​ R v − 1 ‖ 2 ​ 𝑑 v ≤ 2 ​ 2 g ​ ‖ E ‖ 2 , \displaystyle\|Q(X+E)-Q(X)\|_{2}=\Big\|\int_{0}^{1}\dot{Q}_{v}\,\mathrm{d}v\Big\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|ER_{v}^{-1}\|_{2}\,\mathrm{d}v\leq rac{2\sqrt{2}}{g}\|E\|_{2}, (22) where we used ‖ E ​ R v − 1 ‖ 2 ≤ ‖ E ‖ 2 ​ ‖ R v − 1 ‖ ∞ \|ER_{v}^{-1}\|_{2}\leq\|E\|_{2}\|R_{v}^{-1}\|_{\infty} in the last inequality. ∎ For operations specified by an isometry matrix, the following lemma gives a finite circuit with explicit error and gate bounds. The construction eliminates the subdiagonal entries by two-level unitaries, and the error analysis accounts for both numerical rounding and finite-gate synthesis. Lemma 16 (Finite-precision isometry synthesis) . Let V : ℂ q → ℂ d V:{\mathbb{C}}^{q}	o{\mathbb{C}}^{d} be an isometry, where 1 ≤ q ≤ d 1\leq q\leq d , and let δ ∈ ( 0 , 1 / 2 ) \delta\in(0,1/2) . Given a rational matrix A 0 A_{0} satisfying ‖ A 0 − V ‖ 2 ≤ δ / 128 \|A_{0}-V\|_{2}\leq\delta/128 , there is a classical algorithm that constructs a unitary circuit whose first q q columns, denoted by V ^ \widehat{V} , satisfy ‖ V ^ − V ‖ ∞ ≤ δ  ig\|\widehat{V}-V ig\|_{\infty}\leq\delta , where the circuit acts on a register of dimension at most 2 ​ d 2d and V V is extended by zero rows to that dimension. The gate count is 𝒪 ⁡ ( d 2 ​ log 3 ⁡ ( 2 ​ d ) ​ log 4 ⁡ ( d / δ ) ) {\mathcal{O}} ig(d^{2}\log^{3}{(2d)}\log^{4}{(d/\delta)} ig) , and the classical running time is polynomial in d d , log ⁡ ( 1 / δ ) \log{(1/\delta)} , and the bit length of ( A 0 , δ ) (A_{0},\delta) . Proof of Lemma 16 . Given a description of A 0 A_{0} , we apply to it the standard elimination by two-level unitaries [ 53 , Sec. 4.5.1] . To this end, we choose the precision parameters as follows: z ≔ δ 256 ​ d 3 , b ≔ δ 256 ​ d 2 . \displaystyle z\coloneqq rac{\delta}{256d^{3}},\qquad b\coloneqq rac{\delta}{256d^{2}}. (23) We eliminate the entries of A 0 A_{0} below the diagonal, column by column, by rotations acting on a pivot pair ( α , β ) (\alpha, eta) consisting of the diagonal entry and the entry to be eliminated. At each such pair, we compare the rational number | α | 2 + | β | 2 |\alpha|^{2}+| eta|^{2} with z 2 z^{2} . If the value is below z 2 z^{2} , we set the stored entry β  eta to zero without applying a rotation. Otherwise, we store a description of the exact two-level rotation G ⁡ ( α , β ) = 1 | α | 2 + | β | 2 ​ ( α ∗ β ∗ − β α ) , \displaystyle G(\alpha, eta)= rac{1}{\sqrt{|\alpha|^{2}+| eta|^{2}}} egin{pmatrix}\alpha^{*}& eta^{*}\ - eta&\alpha\end{pmatrix}, (24) which maps the pair ( α , β ) (\alpha, eta) to ( | α | 2 + | β | 2 , 0 ) (\sqrt{|\alpha|^{2}+| eta|^{2}},\,0) . We compute the corresponding row update with error at most b b in the Hilbert–Schmidt norm and preserve structural zeros exactly. Let A j A_{j} be the working matrix after j j steps. Let Q j Q_{j} be the product of the exact rotations selected through step j j , where a rotation is extended by the identity on the rows it does not act on, and a skipped pair contributes the identity. We write N skip N_{\mathrm{skip}} and N rot N_{\mathrm{rot}} for the numbers of skipped and rotated pivot pairs. At step j j , the working matrix A j A_{j} differs from A j − 1 A_{j-1} by at most z z if the pair is skipped, and from G j ​ A j − 1 G_{j}A_{j-1} by at most b b if a rotation G j G_{j} is applied. Since the subsequent exact rotations preserve the Hilbert–Schmidt norm, the accumulated error is bounded as ‖ A j − Q j ​ V ‖ 2 ≤ ‖ A 0 − V ‖ 2 + N skip ​ z + N rot ​ b ≤ δ 128 + d 2 ​ z + d 2 ​ b ≤ δ 64 , \displaystyle\|A_{j}-Q_{j}V\|_{2}\leq\|A_{0}-V\|_{2}+N_{\mathrm{skip}}z+N_{\mathrm{rot}}b\leq rac{\delta}{128}+d^{2}z+d^{2}b\leq rac{\delta}{64}, (25) where the number of pivot pairs is at most d 2 d^{2} . The working entries remain bounded by two, and every nontrivial pivot denominator is at least z z . The row updates thus require 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( d / δ ) ) {\mathcal{O}}(\log{(d/\delta)}) bits of precision. We convert this bound into an error of the isometry. Let ϵ ≔ δ 64 \epsilon\coloneqq rac{\delta}{64} , let J J be the final step, and write A J = ( T 0 ) A_{J}= inom{T}{0} with T T upper triangular of size q q . Setting E ≔ Q J † ​ A J − V E\coloneqq Q_{J}^{\dagger}A_{J}-V , the bound above reads ‖ E ‖ 2 ≤ ϵ \|E\|_{2}\leq\epsilon , and the minimum singular value σ min ​ ( V ) = 1 \sigma_{\min}(V)=1 gives σ min ​ ( T ) = σ min ​ ( A J ) ≥ 1 − ϵ \sigma_{\min}(T)=\sigma_{\min}(A_{J})\geq 1-\epsilon . The inverse T − 1 T^{-1} is upper triangular with the diagonal entries T j ​ j − 1 T_{jj}^{-1} , and hence | T j ​ j | − 1 ≤ ‖ T − 1 ‖ ∞ ≤ ( 1 − ϵ ) − 1 |T_{jj}|^{-1}\leq\|T^{-1}\|_{\infty}\leq(1-\epsilon)^{-1} . An error in T j ​ j T_{jj} is amplified by 1 / | T j ​ j | 1/|T_{jj}| in its phase T j ​ j / | T j ​ j | T_{jj}/|T_{jj}| , so this bound keeps the phase evaluation stable and requires polynomially many bits. Writing U ≔ ( P ​ Q J ) † U\coloneqq(PQ_{J})^{\dagger} , we have V + E = Q J † ​ A J = U ​ ( P ​ T 0 ) , \displaystyle V+E=Q_{J}^{\dagger}A_{J}=U inom{PT}{0}, (26) where P ​ T PT is upper triangular with positive diagonal. Since Q ⁡ ( V ) = V Q(V)=V and σ min ​ ( V ) = 1 \sigma_{\min}(V)=1 , Lemma 15 gives ‖ Q ⁡ ( V + E ) − V ‖ 2 ≤ 2 ​ 2 ​ ϵ \|Q(V+E)-V\|_{2}\leq 2\sqrt{2}\epsilon . For finite-gate synthesis, we fix the phase of the implementation by the convention above. We reserve one unused coordinate on which to place the compensating phase, and pad the matrix register to dimension 2 ⌈ log ⁡ ( d + 1 ) ⌉ ≤ 2 ​ d 2^{\lceil\log{(d+1)}ceil}\leq 2d . The extension is hence a determinant-one unitary, and its determinant phase is computed from the selected rotations and row phases. The unitary U U is a product of two-level factors, and the compensating phase can be absorbed into one of them, so the extension is a product of two-level special unitaries. Following Ref. [ 54 , Secs. 7–8] , these are decomposed into 𝒪 ⁡ ( d 2 ​ log 3 ⁡ ( 2 ​ d ) ) {\mathcal{O}}(d^{2}\log^{3}{(2d)}) elementary gates acting on the matrix register alone. The following lemma implements one with finite precision. Its guarantee is not that the output circuit is drawn from a distribution close to the Haar measure: the circuit and an exact Haar unitary are defined on a common probability space, and their actions on inputs with initialized work registers are close on each realization, except with a prescribed failure probability. Lemma 17 (Finite-precision Haar unitary synthesis) . For an integer q ≥ 1 q\geq 1 and δ , ζ H ∈ ( 0 , 1 / 2 ) \delta,\zeta_{\mathrm{H}}\in(0,1/2) , set d 𝖢 ≔ 2 ⌈ log ⁡ ( q + 1 ) ⌉ d_{\mathsf{C}}\coloneqq 2^{\lceil\log{(q+1)}ceil} . On the probability space of its random bits, there is a Haar unitary V 𝖢 V^{\mathsf{C}} on the span of q q fixed vectors of the computational basis in 𝖢 {\mathsf{C}} , extended by the identity on its complement, such that ‖ V ^ 𝖢𝖶 ​ ( 𝕀 𝖢 ⊗ | 0 ⟩ 𝖶 ) − V 𝖢 ⊗ | 0 ⟩ 𝖶 ‖ ∞ ≤ δ , \displaystyle\Big\|\widehat{V}^{{\mathsf{C}}{\mathsf{W}}} ig({\mathbb{I}}^{\mathsf{C}}\otimes|0angle^{\mathsf{W}} ig)-V^{\mathsf{C}}\otimes|0angle^{\mathsf{W}}\Big\|_{\infty}\leq\delta, (29) except with probability at most ζ H \zeta_{\mathrm{H}} . sections.heading: Appendix B Preparatory lemmas for achievability
sections.text: The two appendices that follow present two distillation protocols, and we collect here the material they share. We briefly explain the Schur–Weyl duality in Sec. B.1 , and reduce the error of the distilled pairs by a concatenated stabilizer code in Sec. B.2 .

sections.heading: B.1 Schur–Weyl duality
sections.text: Let ℋ {\mathcal{H}} be a Hilbert space of dimension d d , and let l ≥ 1 l\geq 1 be an integer. The Schur–Weyl decomposition [ 57 , 58 ] of l l copies of ℋ {\mathcal{H}} reads ℋ ⊗ l ≅ ⨁ λ ⊢ l 𝒲 λ ​ ( d ) ⊗ 𝒮 λ , \displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}^{\otimes l}\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash l}{\mathcal{W}}_{\lambda}(d)\otimes{\mathcal{S}}_{\lambda}, (35) where λ ⊢ l \lambda\vdash l means that λ \lambda is a partition of l l , 𝒲 λ ​ ( d ) {\mathcal{W}}_{\lambda}(d) is the space of the irreducible representation of the unitary group on ℋ {\mathcal{H}} , which is zero when the number ℓ ⁡ ( λ ) \ell(\lambda) of rows of λ \lambda exceeds d d , and 𝒮 λ {\mathcal{S}}_{\lambda} is that of the symmetric group S l S_{l} of degree l l . We write d λ ≔ dim 𝒮 λ d_{\lambda}\coloneqq\dim{\mathcal{S}}_{\lambda} , and Π λ \Pi_{\lambda} for the projector onto the λ \lambda sector, carrying the register of ℋ {\mathcal{H}} as a superscript where several registers appear. The unitaries U ⊗ l U^{\otimes l} act as the identity on 𝒮 λ {\mathcal{S}}_{\lambda} , and more generally we write π λ ​ ( X ) \pi_{\lambda}(X) for the action of X ⊗ l X^{\otimes l} on 𝒲 λ ​ ( d ) {\mathcal{W}}_{\lambda}(d) , so that Π λ ​ X ⊗ l ​ Π λ = π λ ​ ( X ) ⊗ 𝕀 𝒮 λ \Pi_{\lambda}X^{\otimes l}\Pi_{\lambda}=\pi_{\lambda}(X)\otimes{\mathbb{I}}^{{\mathcal{S}}_{\lambda}} . The permutations of the l l copies act as the identity on 𝒲 λ ​ ( d ) {\mathcal{W}}_{\lambda}(d) and irreducibly on 𝒮 λ {\mathcal{S}}_{\lambda} . By Schur–Weyl duality, the operators commuting with every U ⊗ l U^{\otimes l} are those of the form ⨁ λ 𝕀 𝒲 λ ​ ( d ) ⊗ X λ \bigoplus_{\lambda}{\mathbb{I}}^{{\mathcal{W}}_{\lambda}(d)}\otimes X_{\lambda} , and they are spanned by the permutations. We pad a Hilbert space with unused basis states whenever a construction requires its dimension to take a particular value. Such a padding is a local isometric embedding, and it leaves the nonzero eigenvalues of every state, its rank, and its entanglement unchanged. At d ≥ l d\geq l , every λ ⊢ l \lambda\vdash l appears in Eq. ( 35 ), since ℓ ⁡ ( λ ) ≤ l \ell(\lambda)\leq l .

sections.heading: B.2 Error reduction by a concatenated code
sections.text: Each of the two protocols produces polynomially many pairs of qubits with a small infidelity, and the infidelity accumulates over the pairs. We here reduce the error by a QECC, which allows the final error of each protocol to be made exponentially small. The QECC we use is a concatenated stabilizer code [ 59 , 60 ] . A short inner code is decoded by a table listing a correction for each syndrome, and an algebraic outer code repairs the inner blocks on which that table fails. We choose the inner code as a Clifford code sampled approximately uniformly at random, which requires no code search or distance certification and whose table is built in polynomial time in both distillation protocols. Both codes act as one-way distillation protocols. To see this, we recall the transpose trick of the maximally entangled state | Φ ⟩ 𝖠𝖡 |\Phi\rangle^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} , which gives ( ( V ⊤ ) 𝖠 ⊗ ( V † ) 𝖡 ) ​ ( 𝕀 𝖠 ⊗ E 𝖡 ) ​ | Φ ⟩ 𝖠𝖡 = ( 𝕀 𝖠 ⊗ ( V † ​ E ​ V ) 𝖡 ) ​ | Φ ⟩ 𝖠𝖡 . \displaystyle\big(\big(V^{\top}\big)^{\mathsf{A}}\otimes\big(V^{\dagger}\big)^{\mathsf{B}}\big)\big({\mathbb{I}}^{\mathsf{A}}\otimes E^{\mathsf{B}}\big)|\Phi\rangle^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}}=\big({\mathbb{I}}^{\mathsf{A}}\otimes\big(V^{\dagger}EV\big)^{\mathsf{B}}\big)|\Phi\rangle^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}}. (36) Here, V V and V † V^{\dagger} can be regarded as encoding and decoding unitaries, and E E as an error operator. In particular, when V V is Clifford and E E is Pauli, the conjugated error V † ​ E ​ V V^{\dagger}EV is again a Pauli operator. Alice and Bob apply V ⊤ V^{\top} and V † V^{\dagger} , respectively, and both measure the check qubits; Alice then sends her outcomes. Their difference is the syndrome of the conjugated error, which Bob corrects [ 3 , 61 ] . The stabilizer formalism and the action of Clifford unitaries on Pauli operators are reviewed, e.g., in Ref. [ 62 , Chaps. 3 and 4] . In the following, we deal with pairs of qubits, one held by Alice and the other by Bob. The two codes act on such pairs, and the target of each of them is the Bell state Φ 2 \Phi_{2} . All communication goes from Alice to Bob, and neither the input state nor any description of it enters the construction. The construction is controlled by two parameters, a rate loss a a shared by the two codes and the length N N of the outer code. The length L L of the inner code is then determined by a a and N N , and the error of the output decreases exponentially in N N . Lemma 18 (Error reduction by a concatenated code) . Let a ∈ ( 0 , 1 / 32 ] a\in(0,1/32] and ζ c ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \zeta_{\mathrm{c}}\in(0,1) , and let N N and S S be integers such that N ≥ 4 / a N\geq 4/a and S ≥ 1 S\geq 1 . (38) Then, there is a one-way LOCC protocol that consumes S S code blocks of k c k_{\mathrm{c}} pairs each and outputs S ​ m c Sm_{\mathrm{c}} pairs. Its inner code is a random Clifford code drawn at each use of the protocol, and its outer code is computed from a a and N N by a classical randomized algorithm that succeeds with probability at least 1 − ζ c 1-\zeta_{\mathrm{c}} ; when this algorithm fails, the protocol returns a fixed state of the same size. The following statements hold. 1. Suppose that, within each code block, the state is a product across its k c k_{\mathrm{c}} pairs, each of which has fidelity at least 1 − u c 1-u_{\mathrm{c}} with Φ 2 \Phi_{2} . We first describe the inner code and bound the probability that an inner block carries a logical error, then describe the outer code and bound the failure probability of one code block, and finally collect the lengths and the costs. For each i = 1 , … , N i=1,\ldots,N , Alice draws a uniform L L -qubit Clifford V c V_{\mathrm{c}} , independently for distinct i i , and sends the seed that specifies it; the same V c V_{\mathrm{c}} is used at the i i -th inner block of every code block, so that N N seeds are drawn in total. ( 37 ) and λ c ≥ 9 \lambda_{\mathrm{c}}\geq 9 . The table is therefore built without enumerating all 4 L 4^{L} Pauli errors. For a fixed actual error of weight at most v c v_{\mathrm{c}} , the product of the two Paulis in a collision is a fixed nonidentity Pauli, which for a uniform s c s_{\mathrm{c}} -dimensional stabilizer lies in the normalizer with probability ( 2 2 ​ L − s c − 1 ) / ( 2 2 ​ L − 1 ) ≤ 2 1 − s c (2^{2L-s_{\mathrm{c}}}-1)/(2^{2L}-1)\leq 2^{1-s_{\mathrm{c}}} [ 7 , Chap. 24] . The protocol need not identify such an inner block. We turn to the outer code, which treats each inner block as a symbol of w c w_{\mathrm{c}} qubits. Since w c ≥ L / 2 w_{\mathrm{c}}\geq L/2 , we have 2 w c ≥ N + 1 2^{w_{\mathrm{c}}}\geq N+1 , and we may work over 𝔽 2 w c {\mathbb{F}}_{2^{w_{\mathrm{c}}}} and choose distinct z 1 , … , z N z_{1},\ldots,z_{N} there. To decode either syndrome, Bob first finds a vector x ^ \hat{x} with that syndrome by Gaussian elimination, so that x ^ − x ∈ 𝒢 ⟂ \hat{x}-x\in{\mathscr{G}}^{\perp} for the true error x x . After dividing the coordinates of x ^ \hat{x} by ς i \varsigma_{i} , he applies the Welch–Berlekamp decoder with dimension N − r c N-r_{\mathrm{c}} and radius ⌊ r c / 2 ⌋ \lfloor r_{\mathrm{c}}/2\rfloor , restores the multipliers, and subtracts the decoded codeword from x ^ \hat{x} . The algorithm, its correctness, and its 𝒪 ⁡ ( N 3 ) {\mathcal{O}}(N^{3}) field-operation bound are Ref. [ 65 , Algorithm 12.1.1 and Theorems 12.1.3 and 12.1.6] . Code blocks may remain correlated, both through the shared seeds and through their inputs.
