sections.heading: Appendix C Achievability: Universal Schur coding with polynomially many copies
sections.text: We prove sample-efficient entanglement distillation for states close to a state of polynomial rank, without restricting the marginal ranks. The coding and entropy estimates are imported from Ref. [ 29 ] ; we give the additional support-enlargement and perturbation arguments needed for states that are only close to a state of polynomial rank. We present these tools in Sec. C.1 , and combine them into the sample-efficient achievability result in Sec. C.2 .

sections.heading: C.1 Schur coding tools
sections.text: In Sec. C.1.1 , we recall from Ref. [ 29 ] the Schur information spectrum, the Clebsch–Gordan channel picture, and the universal coding bound, which bounds the infidelity by the weight of the information spectrum below a threshold. We bound this weight by the Rényi coherent information in Sec. C.1.2 . In Sec. C.1.3 , we show that a single channel recovers Bell pairs from every permutation-invariant state whose weight lies mostly on an invariant projector of small rank. In Sec. C.1.4 , we enlarge the Schur supports to include deviations on a small fraction of the copies, which makes this recovery stable under perturbations of the input state. These tools are combined in Sec. C.2 , where the remaining error of the distilled pairs is reduced by the concatenated code of Sec. B.2 .

sections.heading: C.2 Sample-efficient achievability result
sections.text: We now combine these tools for a state ρ 𝖠𝖡 \rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} close to a nearby state ρ ^ 𝖠𝖡 \hat{\rho}^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} of low rank. sections.heading: Appendix D Achievability: Collective compression and efficient decoupling
sections.text: The distillation protocol in Appendix C acts on the registers of the shared copies themselves, whose dimension grows with the number of copies. Its recovery is specified through the Kronecker coefficients on these registers, and we do not know how to implement it by a circuit of polynomial size. We now require the nearby state to have polynomial rank on its marginals as well, and under this condition we distill at the same rate by a protocol whose circuit size is polynomial. Alice and Bob each begin by compressing their systems of the shared copies into registers of polynomial dimension, without any description of the state, and every subsequent operation acts on these registers alone. The finite-precision implementations of these operations follow the compilation conventions in Sec. A.3 . We present the building blocks of the protocol in Sec. D.1 , combine them into the distillation protocol in Sec. D.2 , and provide the formal version of Case (II) of Theorem 1 in Sec. D.3 .

sections.heading: D.1 Compression and decoupling tools
sections.text: We present the primitives of our distillation protocol, which we combine in Sec. D.2 . In Sec. D.1.1 , we construct the compression channel and characterize its output on selected copies. We then describe Alice’s two-stage measurement in Sec. D.1.2 , whose first stage retains most of the entropy and whose second stage achieves decoupling, and construct Bob’s decoder in Sec. D.1.3 .

sections.heading: D.1.1 Universal collective compression
sections.text:
Universal compression of quantum states has long been studied [ 67 , 68 , 69 ] . These schemes jointly map the i.i.d. copies into a subspace whose dimension is characterized by the entropy, and do not retain a register for each copy. A per-copy dimension reduction is given in Ref. [ 70 ] , which maps each copy into a register of dimension equal to a given upper bound on the rank, with an exact guarantee for inputs obeying that bound. Our channel also reduces each copy separately, but applies to i.i.d. inputs of arbitrary rank together with an arbitrary reference: its output is close to a truncation of each copy at a random threshold, with an error that does not depend on the input. sections.heading: D.1.3 Bob’s decoder
sections.text: After Alice’s second-stage measurement, we construct Bob’s decoder based on Uhlmann’s theorem [ 23 ] to the canonical purification of the marginal on Alice’s retained register and the environment. Decoupling makes this canonical purification close to a maximally entangled state tensored with a purification of the environment. The following lemma implements this transformation for states specified by a factored operator on a tensor power, with cost polynomial in the dimension of one tensor factor and the number of factors. To provide the statement, we take 𝖣 0 {\mathsf{D}}_{0} to be a register of dimension d 𝖣 0 d_{{\mathsf{D}}_{0}} , a power of two, and set 𝖣 ≔ 𝖣 0 t {\mathsf{D}}\coloneqq{\mathsf{D}}_{0}^{t} . sections.heading: Appendix E Preparatory lemmas for converses
sections.text: We collect here the lemmas needed to establish both converse bounds in Appendices F and G . In Sec. E.1 , we show how the entropies and distillable entanglement of a state constructed from branches under a locally readable flag are determined by those of the branches. In Sec. E.2 , we construct a state whose conditional Rényi entropy can be tuned through its order. In Sec. E.3 , we bound the rate of a distillation protocol at a finite number of copies by dominating the input state with a separable state.

sections.heading: Appendix F Converse: Haar random construction and statistical indistinguishability
sections.text: We here show our converse bounds in the state-agnostic and the state-dependent models, for which no computational hardness assumption is used. We present the tools related to Haar randomness in Sec. F.1 , construct the family of states from them in Sec. F.2 , and prove the bounds on it in Sec. F.3 .

sections.heading: F.1 Haar random tools
sections.text: In this section, we collect the tools related to Haar randomness that we use. Lemma 42 (Haar and Haar-subsystem states on 2 ​ m 2m qubits; adapted from Ref. sections.heading: F.3 Statistical converse result
sections.text: We provide the converse bounds on the state-agnostic and the computational distillable entanglement of Definitions 11 and 12 using the family constructed in the previous subsection. In Sec. F.3.1 , we first consider a single protocol of unrestricted size that must succeed on the whole state set, as in model (M1). In Sec. F.3.2 , we then consider model (M2), in which the protocol may depend on the state in any way but its circuit size is polynomial. In this case, concentration and a union bound select one state against all such protocols. Both models give the same cap. In Sec. F.3.3 , we provide a simplified statement of these bounds in terms of the Rényi coherent information. Each party may additionally receive l = poly ⁡ ( n ) l=\mathrm{poly}(n) copies of a purification, each held entirely in that party’s laboratory, where l l is a nonnegative integer.

sections.heading: Appendix G Converse: Cryptographic construction and efficiently preparable states
sections.text: We provide our converse bounds in the description-aware case, under conjectured cryptographic hardness assumptions. We introduce the cryptographic tools in Sec. G.1 and the public-key pseudoentanglement built from them in Sec. G.2 . We then construct the family of states in Sec. G.3 and prove the bounds on it in Sec. G.4 .

sections.heading: G.1 Cryptographic tools
sections.text: Our converse bounds in the description-aware case rely on two cryptographic ingredients—a lossy function family and a labeled generator—both of which we instantiate from the conjectured hardness of the learning with errors (LWE) decision problem [ 35 ] with binary secrets. We introduce the LWE assumptions in Sec. G.1.1 and the two ingredients in Sec. G.1.2 .

sections.heading: G.1.1 Learning with errors
sections.text: Below, ℓ ≥ 1 \ell\geq 1 denotes the LWE dimension, which plays the role of the security parameter, m m the number of noisy linear equations, q q the modulus, and σ \sigma the standard deviation of the error distribution. We reserve n n for the number of qubits under consideration. Definition 52 (LWE decision problem with binary secrets [ 93 ] ) . Let 𝕌 q m × ℓ {\mathbb{U}}_{q}^{m\times\ell} denote the uniform distribution over ℤ q m × ℓ {\mathbb{Z}}_{q}^{m\times\ell} , and let 𝔻 q , σ m × ℓ {\mathbb{D}}_{q,\sigma}^{m\times\ell} denote the distribution over ℤ q m × ℓ {\mathbb{Z}}_{q}^{m\times\ell} in which every entry is independently sampled from the discretized Gaussian distribution with standard deviation σ \sigma . We write 𝕌 q m ≔ 𝕌 q m × 1 {\mathbb{U}}_{q}^{m}\coloneqq{\mathbb{U}}_{q}^{m\times 1} and 𝔻 q , σ m ≔ 𝔻 q , σ m × 1 {\mathbb{D}}_{q,\sigma}^{m}\coloneqq{\mathbb{D}}_{q,\sigma}^{m\times 1} , and regard { 0 , 1 } ℓ \{0,1\}^{\ell} as a subset of ℤ q ℓ {\mathbb{Z}}_{q}^{\ell} . The LWE ℓ , m , q , σ bin \mathrm{LWE}_{\ell,m,q,\sigma}^{\rm bin} decision problem is the problem of distinguishing the following two distributions over ℤ q m × ℓ × ℤ q m {\mathbb{Z}}_{q}^{m\times\ell}\times{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}^{m} : 1. ( A , u ) ∼ 𝕌 q m × ℓ × 𝕌 q m (A,u)\sim{\mathbb{U}}_{q}^{m\times\ell}\times{\mathbb{U}}_{q}^{m} , 2. ( A , A ​ s + δ ) (A,As+\delta) with A ∼ 𝕌 q m × ℓ A\sim{\mathbb{U}}_{q}^{m\times\ell} , s s uniform on { 0 , 1 } ℓ \{0,1\}^{\ell} , δ ∼ 𝔻 q , σ m \delta\sim{\mathbb{D}}_{q,\sigma}^{m} . The advantage of an algorithm in this problem is the absolute difference of its acceptance probabilities on the two distributions. We say that the LWE ℓ , m , q , σ bin \mathrm{LWE}_{\ell,m,q,\sigma}^{\rm bin} decision problem is ( T , ϵ ) (T,\epsilon) -hard if every family of quantum circuits of size at most T ⁡ ( ℓ ) T(\ell) has advantage at most ϵ ⁡ ( ℓ ) \epsilon(\ell) for all sufficiently large ℓ \ell . We quantify over circuits rather than over uniform algorithms, as is standard when the size and advantage bounds are stated as explicit functions of the security parameter; this is the stronger requirement of the two, and it matches the class of protocols against which our converse bounds are proved. We consider the LWE ℓ , m , q , σ bin \mathrm{LWE}_{\ell,m,q,\sigma}^{\rm bin} decision problem in the regime q = poly ( ℓ + m ) : prime , ℓ 1 / 2 log ℓ ≤ σ < q , \displaystyle q=\mathrm{poly}(\ell+m)\text{: prime},\ \ \ \ \ell^{1/2}\log{\ell}\leq\sigma<q, (277) and invoke its hardness against circuits of superpolynomial size at two numbers of equations m m , polynomially and subexponentially many in ℓ \ell . These are the usual parameter choices for LWE [ 94 ] , except that the lower bound on σ \sigma is raised to a noise level at which the reduction from standard LWE to binary LWE applies [ 93 ] . Assumption 53 (Hardness assumptions for LWE with binary secrets) . We consider the following two assumptions on the quantum hardness of the LWE ℓ , m , q , σ bin \mathrm{LWE}_{\ell,m,q,\sigma}^{\rm bin} decision problem, each required to hold for every ( m , q , σ ) (m,q,\sigma) obeying Eq. ( 277 ) with m m in the range stated in the item. (H1) Hardness at polynomially many equations: there exist constants c 1 , c 2 > 0 c_{1},c_{2}>0 such that, for every m = poly ⁡ ( ℓ ) m=\mathrm{poly}(\ell) , the problem is ( 2 c 1 ​ ℓ / log ⁡ ( 2 + m ​ log ⁡ q / ℓ ) , 2 − c 2 ℓ / log ( 2 + m log q / ℓ ) ) \big(2^{c_{1}\ell/\log(2+m\log{q}/\ell)},\ 2^{-c_{2}\ell/\log(2+m\log{q}/\ell)}\big) -hard. (H2) Hardness at subexponentially many equations: there exist constants 1 > γ 1 > γ 2 > 0 1>\gamma_{1}>\gamma_{2}>0 such that, for every m = 2 𝒪 ⁡ ( ℓ γ 2 ) m=2^{{\mathcal{O}}(\ell^{\gamma_{2}})} , the problem is ( T , 2 − Ω ⁡ ( ℓ γ 1 ) ) \big(T,2^{-\Omega(\ell^{\gamma_{1}})}\big) -hard for every T = 2 𝒪 ⁡ ( ℓ γ 2 ) T=2^{{\mathcal{O}}(\ell^{\gamma_{2}})} . Assumption (H1) is used for the first application of Lemma 58 in Sec. G.3.1 and for the labeled generator of Lemma 57 , and (H2) for the second application there and, in one parameter regime, for the third. The second application makes the information-theoretic distillable entanglement of our family nearly extensive at a subexponential number of equations. At m = poly ⁡ ( ℓ ) m=\mathrm{poly}(\ell) , the exponent in (H1) is Ω ⁡ ( ℓ / log ⁡ ℓ ) \Omega(\ell/\log{\ell}) , and (H1) implies the bound of (H2) there; (H2) adds content only at m m superpolynomial in ℓ \ell , where (H1) asserts nothing. We state both assumptions directly rather than deriving them from the worst-case hardness of lattice problems. The known reduction from standard LWE to LWE with binary secrets [ 93 ] maps dimension k k to dimension Θ ⁡ ( k ​ log ⁡ q ) \Theta(k\log{q}) and increases the noise, and thus does not carry the exponent of (H1) as a function of ℓ \ell . We state the size and advantage bounds explicitly because we shall take ℓ \ell polylogarithmic in n n , against adversaries of size poly ⁡ ( n ) \mathrm{poly}(n) , where hardness polynomial in ℓ \ell and an advantage negligible only in ℓ \ell are insufficient. The dependence of (H1) on m m accommodates known subexponential attacks. For example, for m = 10 ​ ℓ m=10\ell , q = Θ ⁡ ( ℓ 3 ) q=\Theta(\ell^{3}) prime, and σ = ℓ \sigma=\ell , combining the small-secret BKW algorithm of Ref. [ 95 , Theorem 4] with the sample amplification of Ref. [ 96 , Lemma 2] gives an algorithm for our decision problem with running time 2 𝒪 ⁡ ( ℓ / log ⁡ log ​ ℓ ) 2^{{\mathcal{O}}(\ell/\log\log{\ell})} . The exponent in (H1) is Θ ⁡ ( ℓ / log ⁡ log ​ ℓ ) \Theta(\ell/\log\log{\ell}) for this parameter family; a hardness bound 2 Ω ⁡ ( ℓ ) 2^{\Omega(\ell)} uniform over all m = poly ⁡ ( ℓ ) m=\mathrm{poly}(\ell) would therefore be false. At m = Θ ⁡ ( ℓ / log ⁡ ℓ ) m=\Theta(\ell/\log{\ell}) and q = poly ⁡ ( ℓ ) q=\mathrm{poly}(\ell) , the parameters of the labeled generator below, the exponent is Θ ⁡ ( ℓ ) \Theta(\ell) , and the explicit dependence on m m also covers the larger polynomial numbers of equations used by the lossy function family of Lemma 55 . The subexponential scaling of the number of equations and of the circuit size in (H2) also appears in Ref. [ 34 , Assumption 2.19] and Ref. [ 40 , Assumption 3.5] ; the secret, modulus, and noise regimes there differ from ours, and we state (H2) directly in the form used here. We take γ 2 < 1 / 2 \gamma_{2}<1/2 without loss of generality, as (H2) at a constant γ 2 \gamma_{2} implies (H2) at every smaller one. Its circuit size bound 2 𝒪 ⁡ ( ℓ γ 2 ) 2^{{\mathcal{O}}(\ell^{\gamma_{2}})} coincides with poly ⁡ ( m ) \mathrm{poly}(m) at m = 2 Θ ⁡ ( ℓ γ 2 ) m=2^{\Theta(\ell^{\gamma_{2}})} and exceeds it at fewer equations, where we use it as well.

(L1) For k ← 𝒦 n 0 k\leftarrow{\mathcal{K}}_{n}^{0} , the function g k g_{k} is injective with probability 1 − negl ⁡ ( n ) 1-\operatorname{negl}(n) . Contact: takeru-utsumi@g.ecc.u-tokyo.ac.jp, jacopo.rizzo@fu-berlin.de Affiliation: Dahlem Center for Complex Quantum Systems, Freie Universität Berlin, 14195 Berlin, Germany Ryuji Takagi Affiliation: Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, The University of Tokyo, 3-8-1 Komaba, Meguro-ku, Tokyo 153-8902, Japan Lorenzo Leone Affiliation: Dipartimento di Ingegneria Industriale, Università degli Studi di Salerno, Via Giovanni Paolo II, 132, 84084 Fisciano (SA), Italy Affiliation: Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN) Sezione di Napoli, Gruppo Collegato di Salerno, Italy October 5, 2026 Abstract The information-theoretic approach to entanglement typically relies on arbitrarily many input copies and unboundedly complex operations; however, the available resources are constrained in reality. This motivates the study of entanglement theory with limited resources. One of its central questions is which quantities characterize entanglement manipulations, and so far, only the idealized case of pure states has been well explored. In this work, we address entanglement distillation from mixed states and identify the Rényi coherent information as the quantity determining the optimal rate in the worst case under two distinct resource constraints. We first characterize the sample-efficient regime, in which unbounded computational power is allowed. Our universal protocol achieves this rate without knowledge of the input state under certain polynomial rank constraints. This rate is optimal among universal protocols: we construct states whose distillable entanglement is nearly extensive, yet from which no universal sample-efficient protocol attains a rate above their Rényi coherent information. We then push this characterization to the computationally efficient frontier: the same bound holds for any efficient protocol even when the input state is known, and another universal protocol achieves this rate efficiently under additional polynomial constraints on the marginal ranks. Overall, our results give the Rényi coherent information a novel operational meaning in two computational settings: universal distillation with limited copies and efficient distillation even with knowledge of the input state. I Introduction Quantum information theory characterizes the ultimate limits of information processing. Entanglement theory is a prime example: it studies how entanglement, a central resource of quantum information processing, can be quantified and manipulated under local operations and classical communication (LOCC) [ 1 ] . One of its most fundamental tasks is entanglement distillation, which converts multiple copies of a noisy entangled state into nearly perfect Bell pairs [ 2 , 3 ] . Distillation supplies resources for teleportation [ 4 ] , quantum repeaters [ 5 ] , and quantum cryptography [ 6 ] , and lies at the heart of quantum Shannon theory [ 7 ] , closely tied to quantum communication over noisy channels [ 3 ] . Which quantities characterize the optimal asymptotic distillation rate, known as the distillable entanglement, is a central question in entanglement theory. For pure states, this rate is given by the entanglement entropy [ 8 ] . Noisy states, however, are generally mixed, and their distillable entanglement is harder to characterize: a general closed-form expression is unknown, and some entangled states cannot be distilled at all [ 9 ] . The optimal distillation rate can nevertheless be characterized in terms of the coherent information [ 10 , 11 ] . These entropic characterizations, however, describe what is possible in principle rather than what is feasible in practice. Since physical resources are limited, accounting for the cost of manipulating entanglement is crucial. Specifically, what matters is how the number of copies and the complexity of operations scale with the number n n of qubits. Once efficiency is imposed by restricting both to grow polynomially with n n , the picture changes drastically [ 12 , 13 ] . This is illustrated by pseudoentanglement [ 14 ] , which extends quantum pseudorandomness [ 15 ] to entanglement and provides two ensembles with very different amounts of entanglement that no efficient observer can tell apart. Since efficient protocols cannot distinguish these ensembles, there exist states with large distillable entanglement from which they distill only a small amount. Such observations, together with the advance of quantum technologies toward practical use, have motivated computational entanglement theory, which seeks to characterize the limits attainable by efficient protocols and identifies computational counterparts of entanglement measures and entropic quantities [ 16 , 12 , 17 , 13 , 18 ] . For pure states, Leone et al. [ 12 ] recently showed that, with resources polynomial in n n , the optimal distillation rate is characterized in the worst case by the min-entropy of the reduced state rather than its von Neumann entropy. Yet pure states are highly idealized—the natural setting for distillation involves mixed states produced by noise. In the distillation protocol for pure states [ 19 ] on which Ref. [ 12 ] relies, simply measuring the Schur labels of the copies already leaves a maximally entangled state. In contrast, for mixed states we must deal with correlations with the environment, and an additional decoding step is needed to recover Bell pairs. The standard decoupling approach [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] to mixed-state distillation uses Uhlmann’s theorem [ 23 ] to guarantee the existence of a suitable decoder, known as the Uhlmann transformation, but this does not by itself yield an efficient implementation [ 24 ] . From the perspective of fundamental limitations, existing converse bounds indicate large gaps between information-theoretic and efficient distillation, but do not identify the quantity governing the efficient rate [ 25 , 26 ] . These facts leave open questions: how much entanglement can be distilled from mixed states under resource constraints, and which quantity characterizes the optimal rate? We answer these questions by showing that the sandwiched Rényi coherent information [ 27 , 28 ] of an intermediate order β ∈ ( 1 / 2 , 1 ) \beta\in(1/2,1) determines, in the worst case, the optimal distillation rate in two distinct settings with resource constraints. In the first setting, the number of copies is polynomial in the number n n of qubits, while the circuit size is unrestricted. Here we consider universal one-way LOCC distillation, which uses no description of the input state. The universal entanglement distillation was initially considered for pure-state inputs [ 19 ] and has recently been extended to general mixed states [ 29 , 30 , 31 ] . In particular, Rizzo et al. [ 29 ] generalized the protocol for pure states [ 19 ] to universal Schur coding for mixed states. For polynomial-rank states, their protocol achieves rates given by the Rényi coherent information capped at C ​ log ⁡ n C\log{n} for any constant C > 0 C>0 . We further extend this guarantee to any state close to a polynomial-rank state, including a low-rank state subject to weak noise, by making the decoder robust to deviations in a small fraction of the copies. The rate is then determined by the Rényi coherent information of this nearby state. While this protocol is sample-efficient, its efficient implementation remains open. We next turn to the second setting, in which the circuit size is also polynomial in n n . 1 1 1 Computationally efficient protocols are automatically sample-efficient, since a circuit of polynomial size can act on only polynomially many copies. Under the additional condition that the nearby state has polynomial marginal ranks, we obtain another universal one-way LOCC protocol based on decoupling that achieves the Rényi coherent information. Since known implementations of the Uhlmann transformation [ 32 , 33 ] become costly in high dimensions, our key idea is universal collective compression, which reduces the local dimension per copy to a polynomial. Under the marginal-rank condition, the compression loses almost no entanglement. The receiving party then learns the compressed state from some of the copies and efficiently implements the Uhlmann transformation on the others. To establish the optimality of these rates in the worst case, we construct a family of n n -qubit mixed states of polynomial rank whose information-theoretic distillable entanglement is as large as Ω ~ ​ ( n ) \widetilde{\Omega}(n) . For universal LOCC protocols using k = poly ⁡ ( n ) k=\mathrm{poly}(n) copies, the rate is capped by the smaller of the Rényi coherent information and log ⁡ k \log{k} , even when the circuit size is unrestricted. Its main ingredient is statistical indistinguishability: given polynomially many copies, ensembles constructed from Haar-random states cannot be distinguished from ensembles carrying little entanglement. The Schur-coding protocol nearly matches this bound, attaining the Rényi coherent information up to o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) when it is 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) {\mathcal{O}}(\log{n}) and otherwise a constant fraction of log ⁡ k \log{k} at the number k k of copies it uses. We next turn to the computationally efficient setting, now allowing the protocol to be tailored to the input state, and we show that the same bound holds even in this setting. The states in this construction, however, need not be efficiently preparable, so the bound may be attributed to the complexity of the states themselves [ 16 ] . Computational indistinguishability based on public-key pseudoentanglement [ 34 ] closes this loophole. Under a post-quantum hardness assumption for learning with errors (LWE) [ 35 ] , we construct efficiently preparable states for which a similar bound holds even against protocols efficiently compiled from a description of their preparation circuit, with log ⁡ k \log{k} replaced by a freely chosen function of order ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) \omega(\log{n}) . When the Rényi coherent information is 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) {\mathcal{O}}(\log{n}) , our efficient protocol attains the bound up to o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) without a description of the state. It is therefore optimal even against protocols tailored to the input state or efficiently compiled from a description of its preparation circuit. Our results reveal some features of efficient distillation that are specific to mixed states. First, intermediate Rényi orders are essential for characterizing the optimal rate of efficient distillation from mixed states. The Rényi coherent information at the endpoint β = 1 / 2 \beta=1/2 equals the min-entropy conditioned on the purifying system by the duality relation [ 27 ] . One might expect this endpoint to suffice for mixed states, as the min-entropy does for pure states [ 12 ] . For pure states, the trivial purifying system makes the values at all fixed orders β ∈ [ 1 / 2 , 1 ) \beta\in[1/2,1) agree up to a constant factor, whereas for mixed states these values can separate by an amount growing with the rank. Indeed, we construct polynomial-rank states whose conditional min-entropy is − Θ ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) -\Theta(\log{n}) , yet whose optimal rate of efficient distillation is Θ ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) \Theta(\log{n}) and attained by our efficient protocol up to o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) . More strongly, we find that every order in ( 1 / 2 , 1 ) (1/2,1) captures the optimal rate for some family of our states but misses it for another; hence, no single fixed order characterizes efficient distillation from mixed states. Second, the optimal rate of efficient distillation undergoes a sharp transition as the rank grows from polynomial to superpolynomial. At superpolynomial rank, our construction yields states from which no efficient protocol distills entanglement at all, even though their information-theoretic distillable entanglement remains Ω ~ ​ ( n ) \widetilde{\Omega}(n) . Such a transition was indicated for special classes of states in earlier work [ 25 , 26 ] ; our results establish it for general mixed states in the worst case. Finally, we mention that our results have implications across a broad range of areas in quantum information science. In quantum networks, decoding complexity is a practical bottleneck for distillation [ 36 ] , and noise on shared states is often not fully characterized. Our efficient protocol, which requires no description of the state, is a step toward addressing these problems. Beyond distillation, implementing the Uhlmann transformation in a compressed space may also facilitate decoding in quantum communication, state merging, and quantum information recovery [ 24 , 26 ] . Pseudoentanglement, in turn, connects our mixed-state constructions to quantum cryptography [ 37 ] and to questions of computational complexity in quantum gravity [ 14 , 38 ] , where mixed states play a central role [ 16 , 39 ] . Together, our protocols and constructions provide tools for investigating how resource constraints shape entanglement manipulation and its applications. Below, we outline how the two protocols are constructed: (I) extends universal Schur coding to perturbed inputs, while (II) makes the decoupling approach efficient by first compressing the local systems of the copies. For details, see Appendix C for (I) and Appendix D for (II). For (I), we start from the universal Schur coding of Ref. [ 29 ] . Alice and Bob apply the Schur transform to their copies and measure the local Schur labels. Alice then measures her symmetric-group register, keeping a register of smaller dimension, and sends her label and the outcome to Bob, who applies a decoder determined by the two labels and this outcome, independent of the input state. The labels select subspaces, the Schur supports, whose permutation symmetry makes the local marginals flat, allowing one decoder to work uniformly on each support; the Rényi coherent information controls the weight outside them. From polynomially many copies of polynomial-rank states, this protocol distills at the Rényi coherent information, capped at order log ⁡ n \log{n} [ 29 ] . Our contribution to (I) is to extend this guarantee to inputs that are only close to a polynomial-rank state and may themselves have large rank. The guarantee for the nearby state does not transfer directly: a small deviation in each copy accumulates, and the tensor powers ρ ⊗ k \rho^{\otimes k} and ρ ^ ⊗ k \hat{\rho}^{\otimes k} can be far apart for polynomially many copies. We instead enlarge the Schur supports to include deviations on a small fraction of the copies, and bound both the size of the enlargement and the weight remaining outside the enlarged supports ( Lemma 23 ). A single decoder then distills from every such input at the rate of the nearby state, still from polynomially many copies ( Lemma 22 ). Finally, a concatenated stabilizer code suppresses the remaining error ( Lemma 18 ). The decoder, however, is specified through Kronecker coefficients on spaces whose dimension grows with the number of copies, and an efficient implementation remains open. For (II), we start from a different approach based on decoupling [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . In this approach, Alice applies a random measurement, retains a register 𝖲 {\mathsf{S}} , and sends the outcome to Bob. The decoupling theorem [ 22 ] guarantees that 𝖲 {\mathsf{S}} is approximately completely mixed and decoupled from the purifying system when its size is chosen according to the Rényi coherent information. Uhlmann’s theorem [ 23 ] then guarantees a decoder on Bob’s systems, the Uhlmann transformation, that recovers Bell pairs shared with 𝖲 {\mathsf{S}} . Known algorithms for this transformation [ 32 , 33 ] , however, become exponentially costly when applied directly to the original high-dimensional systems. To resolve this problem, our first step is universal collective compression ( Lemma 25 ). Alice and Bob reduce the local dimension per copy to a polynomial without learning the original eigenbases. The marginal-rank condition ensures that this compression preserves the nearby state, up to local isometries and a small error. The parties perform local tomography on some of these compressed copies, and Alice sends her outcomes to Bob so that he can estimate the joint compressed state. However, compression alone does not yet make the decoding efficient: decoupling many compressed copies jointly would produce exponentially many outcomes, and the cost of Bob’s decoder grows with their number. Alice thus measures in two stages ( Lemmas 28 and 29 ): she first shrinks each compressed copy separately, retaining its conditional entropy, and then decouples a block of the shrunken copies with only polynomially many outcomes. For the reported outcome, Bob computes the Uhlmann transformation from his estimate as the unitary factor of a polar decomposition. The tensor-product structure of the estimate allows this transformation to be implemented at a cost polynomial in the dimension of one compressed copy and the block length, without constructing a matrix on the full block explicitly ( Lemma 30 ). Finally, a concatenated stabilizer code again suppresses the remaining error. Together, these steps incur only o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) rate loss, and the protocol thus attains the rate in (II) with polynomially many copies and a polynomial-size circuit. All communication goes from Alice to Bob, and the circuit is computed from the promised rank bounds, the target rate, and the target error. II.2 Converse: No-go results and optimality We now ask whether a different protocol can substantially improve these rates. Our converse results construct a family of states with large information-theoretic distillable entanglement but much lower rates under the resource constraints. To state what these bounds rule out, we also need to specify how a protocol may depend on the input state. We distinguish the following three models; see Definition 10 for the formal definition. • State-agnostic. A single protocol is required to succeed on every state in a prescribed set, without information about which member it receives. Its circuit size is unrestricted. • State-dependent. The protocol has polynomial circuit size and may depend on the state in any way; no account is taken of how the circuit is found. • Description-aware. An efficient compiler receives a classical description of a circuit C 𝖠𝖡𝖤 C^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}{\mathsf{E}}} preparing a purification of ρ 𝖠𝖡 \rho^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}} , C 𝖠𝖡𝖤 ​ | 0 ⟩ 𝖠𝖡𝖤 = | ρ ⟩ 𝖠𝖡𝖤 C^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}{\mathsf{E}}}|0\rangle^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}{\mathsf{E}}}=|\rho\rangle^{{\mathsf{A}}{\mathsf{B}}{\mathsf{E}}} , and outputs an efficient LOCC protocol. Thus, moving from state-agnostic to state-dependent models restricts computation while allowing arbitrary dependence on the state; the description-aware model further accounts for the cost of constructing the protocol. The bounds in the three models rest on different types of indistinguishability: statistical in the first two, discussed in Appendix F , and computational in the third, discussed in Appendix G . In the first two models, the amplifier and its counterpart are drawn from Haar-random states and Haar-subsystem states, respectively, which cannot be distinguished from polynomially many copies, regardless of computational power [ 12 ] . Hence, the bounds in these models require no hardness assumption. In the state-agnostic model, where a single protocol must work throughout the state set, this indistinguishability alone gives the first entry of the cap, with no restriction on the circuit size. In the state-dependent model, the protocol may instead be tailored to a single state, and the bound then requires one state that defeats every such protocol. We select such a hard instance from the same set by concentration of measure and a union bound over polynomial-size circuits, which is where the circuit-size restriction enters. In the description-aware model, the compiler also receives a preparation-circuit description, so statistical indistinguishability of the copies alone does not suffice. Under the LWE hardness assumptions, public-key pseudoentanglement [ 34 , 40 ] instead supplies computational indistinguishability even given these descriptions. 5 5 5 The LWE assumptions are imposed at superpolynomial strength, and for binary secrets, to cover the widest parameter ranges.
